It is indeed fitting for us to approach your martyrdom, both for you and for the blessed Stephen, and to signify in this manner every <term>struggle</term><note>original: *athlesis*. Early Christian writers often used athletic metaphors, describing martyrs as "athletes of Christ."</note> of his contests. But how shall we speak of the crown of the first martyr, or how can our voice be found to speak according to his worth? For who should not be moved to praise the blessed man, whose very name alone reveals the proper significance of his person? <note>The author is making a wordplay on the name Stephen, which in Greek (*Stephanos*) literally means "crown."</note> Having in his name the honor already proclaimed—the name of the martyr—revealing the blessed and honorable secret. For is not the crown won immediately after the first of the struggles? And he made his struggle both the path and the door. For this was the first of his honors: the swiftness of his martyrdom. This alone is the wonder: that having run to the door, he should be called by a miracle. His spirit was hemmed in by blood, or rather they went forth by the power of the Father; but he knew the lesson learned from those struggles. He was the first to suffer these things at the hands of the Jews themselves. For You did not abandon us, seeing the entanglements, having appeared as a helper. For such was the blessed contest; he held toward his own <term>way of life</term><note>original: *politeia*, referring to his spiritual conduct or "heavenly citizenship."</note> the <unclear>vision of those gathering</unclear>.

# + The Chapters of <term>Akindynos</term><note>Gregory Akindynos (c. 1300–1348), a monk and theologian who opposed the distinction between God's essence and His uncreated energies.</note> and <term>Barlaam</term><note>Barlaam the Calabrian (c. 1290–1348), an influential monk whose attacks on the prayer practices of the monks of Mount Athos sparked the Hesychast controversy.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Those who oppose the divine Scripture and all the holy teachers say that God does not possess grace, nor any <term>natural operation</term><note>original: *energeia physike*. In this context, it refers to God's activities or "energies" that reach the world, distinct from His hidden essence.</note> whatsoever.

<margin>2</margin> They say that the <term>divine essence</term><note>original: *theia ousia*. The inner, unknowable nature of God.</note> and the <term>nature</term> are the same thing and are called such by everyone. But if anything is called the <term>grace</term> of God, they say it is <term>created</term><note>original: *ktiste*. The core of the debate: if grace is "created," then man is not truly united with God himself, but only with a product of God.</note>, not uncreated; nor is there any such thing as <term>life</term> in the divine nature.

<margin>3</margin> They say again that He has something uncreated, and other things created. And that which is uncreated is the "first <term>unbegotten</term>" <note>original: *agenneton*. Referring here to the Father.</note>. But all things outside of this are either <term>natural</term> or other creations. — Then, changing their position, they say again that this so-called <term>uncreated operation</term> of God—which the saints speak of—is actually the essence of God itself, into which they admit no difference or divine distinction; hence, they claim it is the same thing.

<margin>4</margin> They say the grace of the Spirit—the theology of the <term>Holy Trinity</term>—which is given by Christ to all the faithful, is for all the sacred mysteries of the Christians. They say first and only that man is composed [of these]; again they say that it is created, but that we call it created just as we call Him the Creator.

<margin>5</margin> They say again that this grace of the <term>divinity</term>, which <unclear>p...</unclear>

<column-break/>

...which He also breathed upon and gave to His apostles after the <unclear>Resurrection</unclear>, and which we Christians receive in baptism and the other sacred mysteries—this is merely the opinion and decree of the Scripture, not something proceeding and given by God to the holy ones.

<margin>Note</margin> From this and because of this, they assert a sin and a blasphemy: that the saints do not become partakers of grace, but of the very essence of God itself. <note>The author is accusing his opponents of a logical trap: if grace is the same as essence, then anyone receiving grace is "becoming God" in essence, which is impossible.</note>

<margin>Note</margin> They say that the <term>name</term> of <term>divinity</term> is shared. By this <term>name</term>, they say divinity is attributed similarly to <term>demons</term>, <term>angels</term>, and <term>men</term> by all the holy theologians. They say that all the divine names are spoken of God based on things with souls or things without souls; and because of this, we know and speak of "God" through names, and for this reason He is also <term>nameless</term><note>original: *anonymos*. The idea that God is beyond all human vocabulary.</note>.

<margin>8</margin> They say that there is a <term>difference</term> between His <term>essence</term> and His <term>operation</term>, and that He is one thing while another thing follows Him; hence He would be <term>composite</term><note>original: *synthetos*. A "composite" God was a major theological error, as God must be "simple."</note> from <term>accidents</term><note>original: *symbebekota*. In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of a thing. The author argues that his opponents' logic makes God a collection of parts.</note>, namely essence and <term>operation</term>.

<margin>9</margin> They say that the divine <term>light</term> that shone from Christ at the <term>Transfiguration</term> is the <term>nature</term> of the <term>only-begotten</term> Son of God, and they say it was visible then to the apostles. Then, changing their minds, they say again that the <term>light</term> was <term>created</term>, like a kind of image or apparition. For this reason, it was divided and appeared only for a moment, and because of this, it was <term>annihilated</term>.

<margin>10</margin> They say that the <term>habit</term><note>original: *hexis*. A stable disposition or quality of character.</note> of virtue, which is perfected by men who have achieved it, is called <term>divine grace</term> and...

<meta>This page continues the theological defense against the opponents of the Palamite movement (specifically Barlaam and Akindynos). Page 6 expands this by looking at how the "persons" (hypostases) relate to their "nature" and "energy," drawing heavily on the authority of Gregory of Nyssa to prove that divine activities are inseparable from the divine nature.</meta>

# # Contemplation: —

That their activity <note>original: energeia. In this context, it refers to the outward actions or "rays" of God's power, as opposed to His hidden essence.</note> is but a little thing. And again, that the activity of the Creator, being universal, is both infinite and impassible. Because of this, we hold that nothing is inferior to the Most High. And this is again a response to the uselessness [charged] against me. The same applies to — 
Animate creation reveals the faith of nature. Not being of a lesser sort, it houses a corresponding character. By that same lot, each nature is characterized. The incomprehensible activity, then, represents the persons of nature. The created thing having been created: —

<margin>† From Saint Gregory of Nyssa: —</margin>
If indeed the "created" happens to some to be a person <note>original: prosōpon. Literally "face," used theologically to mean an individual person or subsistence.</note> (from which it is not possible to speak clearly in part concerning nature, nature being dissolved by the creation). But through a corresponding character, it houses a corresponding character. It is clear to all that natural things belong to corresponding natures. That which is non-existent falls short of the existence of a nature. But if it is divided within itself, not every part [truly] exists.
It is clear that how nature exists is not known [in itself], but rather every activity according to nature. From this, it is understood in each. —

<margin>† From the treatise: —</margin>
For nature provides to all the various divine interpretations; the natural wills are introduced alongside them. Specifically, it is the nature of the Father, according to which He is the Father of all — in name, the divine energy, or the will, or

<column-break/>

that which is corresponding to Himself, just as he said to some regarding the Creator: It is necessary that everything belonging to the nature of the created be related to the will: — But it is lacking again, for God has a more specific kinship with this [nature] according to the Cause: — We say this insofar as we say the "all" exists in those things established for themselves, even if not all [actions] relate to the positions of the persons. Rather, there is one single causal <term>hypostasis</term><note>original: hypostasis. The distinct "personhood" of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, as opposed to their shared "nature" (ousia).</note>. 
Not before the Father. Since if there is a nature of the Better, and the One who is the Only-begotten and heir of the Father, then because of divine things, our faith before the Father has certain defined persons existing in themselves through a person which is able to be named.
And the divine nature, as a whole, is called Father. At other times, Son, and at other times, Holy Spirit. — Behold, thus, those who are now spoken of, who blaspheme worse things by dividing God, might better say that our faith holds the same confession of grace both because of ignorance and because of the chapters agreed upon, as if they were resolved through the faith of Christ. It is not easier to choose one of the two: either that the whole nature guarantees a kinship of certainty, or we shall not cease from that most absurd wickedness again—that the divine is but one person. No one can say the Spirit no longer exists because of some other [reason], since it is necessary that each one does not have a private activity of their own; do they not themselves say that the

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Trinity and divine energies, moving from the philosophical distinctions of Gregory of Nyssa to the scriptural and patristic proofs found in the letters of St. Paul, St. Basil the Great, and St. Sophronius. It focuses specifically on the "Apostolic Blessing" from 2 Corinthians 13:13 as evidence for the shared activity and unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</meta>

in person and in the distinct substances <note>original: hypostases. This refers to the three distinct "persons" of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who share one essence.</note>. But it is only by their powers <note>original: dunamesin. These are the divine capacities or "energies" through which God acts upon the world.</note> that they are found to be graspable by those who contemplate them. And they establish this by saying those things which he [the author] speaks of hereafter. Again, regarding the Holy Spirit—for this purpose—
<margin>the Holy Spirit</margin> it is interpreted according to each essence <note>original: ousian. The "being" or "substance" of a thing.</note>. But His own essence happens to exist elsewhere. Or rather, the Holy Spirit is not part of this [created essence]; for He does not belong to the things related to it, or the things related to Himself; but He exists according to Himself.

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all." <note>original: 2 Corinthians 13:13. This "Apostolic Blessing" is a cornerstone of Trinitarian theology.</note> On the one hand, the grace being given is of God; yet it encompasses glory from the Spirit. For as we are being led through sacred rites toward the Spirit, the gift given by Him—in this way, the Spirit given to us would not merely be a "communion" [in a social sense]. Rather, by participating in you <note>meaning the "you" addressed in the scripture</note> in the Holy Spirit, we possess communion with the Son, and the grace of the Son, and the very communion with the Father. Thus, one single blending <note>original: krasis. A term used to describe the interpenetration of the divine persons.</note> of the Pentecostal group <note>original: pentekados. Likely referring to the company of the Holy Spirit or the nature of the gifts given at Pentecost.</note> is revealed. For he [Paul] does not signify the thing given as a divided difference from each Person, as the Apostle shows that the things divinely ministered are of the same [essence]; He is Himself of Himself.

The holy and blessed Trinity is indivisible, or rather, it is described in relation to itself. And we speak of the relationship to the Son and the Word of God. Or the Holy Spirit; for even if it is confessed in this way, one [Person] encompasses the Father, and the Spirit is not separated from the Son. For the grace is one, being fulfilled for us in the Father through the relationship to the Son; for He is not according to the flesh; but the things being fulfilled are from the Father. —

<column-break/>

The blessed Paul, writing somewhere to those who believe correctly, said: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all." For when we first see the Spirits <note>possibly a scribal error for "the things of the Spirit" or a specific reference to the divine activities</note> in relation to the person <note>original: hypostasin</note> of the Father, and then contemplating in this way, let us see the knowledge of the Father in the Son as being indivisible from the Son and the Holy Spirit of the Godhead; and he [Paul] encompasses this inseparably. The Great Basil <note>St. Basil of Caesarea (330–379 AD), one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" who defined the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity.</note> spoke thus: he says that if one were to divide the gifts given by the grace of the Holy Spirit from the aforementioned goods of the Father... but some are not understood as being in any particular thing; others, being known in Him, are of a kinship with her [the grace]—the Epistle to the Philippians follows the relationship to the Father. —

The grace is the enlightenment. And Sophronius the Confessor <note>St. Sophronius of Jerusalem (560–638 AD), a defender of the doctrine of two wills in Christ and a prominent monk-theologian.</note> says: if they say that this energy <note>original: energeian. The outward action or operation of God.</note> is to me 
<margin>+</margin> a creature, and that the Spirit is such as to be brought into being by the Father; we have stood together [in defense]; but how do you collect "energy"? For he says of "the form of God," that "He took the form of a servant." <note>original: Philippians 2:6-7. The "Kenosis" or self-emptying of Christ.</note> For what is the "form"—is it a work, or a servant, or the nature of a servant? <meta>This page continues the technical theological debate regarding the nature of Divine Grace. Having previously discussed the errors of the Messalians and the Latins, the author now provides a catena (a chain of quotes) from the Church Fathers—specifically Paul the Apostle, John Chrysostom, and Cyril of Alexandria—to prove that "Grace" is a divine gift and energy proceeding from God, rather than the inaccessible Essence of God itself.</meta>

...they argue that there is indeed a gift <note>original: dōron</note> of God, but not... again they say that it is not otherwise the whole Holy Spirit <note>original: pneuma hagion</note>. Constructing their former argument from this, they claim that it is not at all [the essence]; they bring forth and assert that everything [from God] is to be called equal in honor and rank, whether it be a gift of grace <note>original: charisma</note> or any other thing, even where the proper name is not applied. He says rather that through it [grace], it is entirely for all: for grace is called "Grace of God," and sometimes it is called "Grace of the Holy Spirit," and at other times "Grace of the Father and the Son," since their [nature] is one... with God, as the word says, "within Him." Let us hear a few things from the many agreed upon by the saints.

<margin>On the same [subject]</margin>
The Apostle **Paul**, for instance, speaks thus: "Grace <note>original: charis</note> gives enjoyment to those deemed worthy to partake in it, yet it is not a consuming force, for it remains, and that which the partakers possess remains incomprehensible." It is also incorruptible, as if it were an outflowing from Him. And the divine **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" Archbishop of Constantinople (c. 347–407 AD).</note>, in explaining the divine Gospel according to John, says: "For the grace of the Spirit, whenever it enters into the mind and is established there, bubbles up more than any spring; it neither fails nor is it emptied." He stands by this; he who demonstrated both the unceasing nature of the supply and the unspeakable nature of the activity <note>original: energeia</note>, calling it a spring.

<column-break/>

He called God a "river"—and not simply a river, but a flood.
<margin>On the same [subject]</margin>
And again, the same author [Chrysostom], searching the sermon of the same period of explanation, says: "And what am I saying? The whole voyage is called 'water'; wherefore [he calls] the Father of Glory this." And the following from the same: "But far from the world, all the earth," he says, "is already consumed by grace; and is not the natural [supply] spent?" 

Saint **Cyril** <note>St. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 AD), a central figure in defining Christological orthodoxy.</note> also says: "For not all Spirit is at all times grace, nor is the grace with Him all things; but upon us, in whom all the things of God are, as far as the account of the **essence** <note>original: ousia; the fundamental "being" or "substance" of God which remains hidden from humans.</note> goes." Thus, the Spirit is Spirit. We might say that this grace has filled all creation or the defense after the resurrection. For the divine **Paul** says: "Having received the Spirit of adoption" <note>Romans 8:15</note> and the prayer of the calling of the Spirit, a gift which necessarily remains with the Spirit. 

Everywhere, as is fitting, all grace is complete; it is not something else, but it is the whole Holy Spirit that is poured out. He is one with the Father and the Son, and with the apostles and all. These things are according to the word, whether [given] by voluntary wisdom or choice, as is said to them. For they themselves are indwellers, having fallen under their own lack of dogma, who say that all which is holy exists through its own **essence** <note>original: ousia</note>. They say that the Spirit by nature—which Christ gave to the apostles after His own resurrection—does this; this is the **person** <note>original: hypostasis; the distinct "personhood" of the Holy Spirit as one of the Trinity.</note> of the Spirit itself.

<meta>This page continues the technical defense of the distinction between God's Essence and His Energies. Indeed, these [opponents] say this as well—look, just like the Latins—as we have reasonably said, that more of the Spirit is poured out upon <margin>51</margin> the children <note>Referring to the faithful or the apostles</note> through <term>participation</term> <note>original: methexis; the theological concept of humans sharing in divine qualities without becoming God by nature</note>.

<column-break/>

It is not [the divine essence] that is poured out, but the gift of Christ is poured out, the grace of the honey-sweet gift. <meta>Continuing from page 29, which introduced a polemic against the "Azymites" (those who use unleavened bread in the Eucharist) and discussed the calculation of Easter, this page transitions into a deep theological defense of Christ’s dual nature. The author argues that the physical reality of Christ’s body and his human suffering are essential to the "economy" or divine plan of salvation, likely to counter arguments that the material elements of the sacraments are unimportant.</meta>

Him; and how is he not manifest to all, even if <unclear>unwritten</unclear> <note>original: ἀγραφῇ; perhaps referring to oral tradition vs. scripture</note>, yet in truth known in everything? First, he is <unclear>proclaimed</unclear> to all <unclear>sensible things</unclear> <note>perceptible by the senses</note> both through the Law and the Prophets. And if all the <unclear>nations</unclear> and every <unclear>created thing</unclear> within it were shown [to him], it was so that no one might ever be <unclear>scandalized</unclear> by the human and the impoverished things performed by him. How much more did he <unclear>justify</unclear> through his works and his divinity? 

He who <unclear>became</unclear> [present] on earth through the flesh did not <unclear>act</unclear> without divinity; just as those things belonging to his divinity were not <unclear>accomplished</unclear> without a body. But since it was <unclear>necessary</unclear> for the things of his flesh to happen in a human way—<unclear>but in truth</unclear>—for which reason, to all those [focused] on fleshly things, he demonstrated all the works of his divinity through the body. He did this to show himself as God, both by being <unclear>persuaded</unclear> <note>or "convinced/proven"</note> through human sufferings <term>pathos<gloss>suffering or passion; the physical experiences of Christ</gloss></term>, and by being confessed as God through them. It was not that he did not undergo human experiences, but that he was <unclear>shown</unclear> to be himself—impassible <note>unable to suffer in his divine nature</note>—through the things [suffered] according to the passion of the one who suffered. This was so he might show the <unclear>mortal</unclear> [clothed] in incorruption <term>aphtharsia<gloss>the state of being not subject to decay or death</gloss></term>, and death <unclear>swallowed up</unclear> in life; so that by the passion through the flesh, he might lead all humanity back to the Father through the Man [Christ]. Thus, the same one is shown to be God in the flesh and to all with his [human] properties, so that he is the same <unclear>God</unclear>.

As it is not <unclear>possible</unclear> <unclear>for the Lord</unclear> to have <unclear>enacted</unclear> all the works of divinity while being [merely] <unclear>tested</unclear>; so that he first <unclear>appears</unclear> to all of us through the mysteries of the same body and to all people, in order to show himself as the true God. And so that through all men, his nature of the flesh [might be known], while the nature of the divinity [is known] in the body. <meta>The previous page concluded a theological defense of Christ’s physical suffering and divine nature. This page (Page 31) serves as the formal opening of the "Bibliotheca" (or Myriobiblon), a massive 9th-century compilation of book summaries. It includes the famous introductory letter from Photius to his brother Tarasius, explaining that these summaries were written at Tarasius's request while Photius was preparing for a dangerous diplomatic mission to the Arab (Abbasid) court.</meta>

# 25. Eulogius. <note>This heading refers to the 25th entry in Photius's collection, concerning the works of Eulogius of Alexandria.</note>

In this very anthology of the Library, containing
summaries of those things in the Holy Scriptures
which have been interpreted allegorically <note>Reading the Bible for symbolic or spiritual meanings</note> and explained
according to historical fact, as well as various
other matters; to which are also attached
his own genuine discourses, which he sent
to his most sweet brother, Tarasius.

---

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative headpiece (pyle) featuring an ornate border of interlocking geometric and vine patterns. The center contains nine circular medallions arranged in a three-by-three grid, each filled with stylized floral rosettes. Small floral finials extend from the top corners.</image-desc>

->From our most holy and most wise father Photius, Archbishop of Constantinople, to Tarasius, his most beloved brother.<-

Would that we, O most beloved child and brother, were able to enjoy your most dear and shared presence and conversation—especially since we have been appointed by the imperial and common vote to an embassy <note>original: πρεσβείαν; Photius was sent on a diplomatic mission to the Caliph at Baghdad</note>, even though we did not wish for it. But the storm of our sins <note>A common Byzantine expression of humility, attributing misfortune to one's own failings</note> has prevailed to such an extent that it has separated me from you, and thus I must make this journey to a dwelling far removed from our life together. Indeed, if fortune had shown me [this], except that this too was reserved for me along with other evils; but since the purpose of this journey has fallen upon us according to what was granted to you, you have seen fit to ask me to write down, in the form of summaries, the contents of those books which we went through while you were not present.

Since we began these readings after your departure, even if they happen to be many in number, I shall nevertheless provide these summary notes and descriptions of them—not because I consider your own reasoning to be of no account, as my mind has often thought, but rather to fulfill what is lacking in your comfort, as if for a sacred mission. I must first promise what is at hand, as we are not able to provide a narrative and the fulfillment of the need with the respect that is due. For not long after your departure, almost all the contents [of the books] were stored away in my memory, as if in private, through those things we worked on individually. As for those things which need not be unclear, it would be the right time to learn them before our meeting. Since the notebook volume <note>original: δελτὸς τόμος; likely referring to the manuscript Photius used to record his notes</note> says there are two hundred and twenty-five <note>original: πέντε καὶ εἴκοσι καὶ διακοσίων; modern editions usually contain 279 or 280 entries</note> works, as many as we read after your departure, you have asked me to set these out.

We have said that our most man-loving Master and God, expecting to provide some comfort during our absence, as it seems, allows us to be consoled by this conversation through letters even before our meeting. Accept, then, what has been written. And if by some chance we should fail in any of the previously set out accounts, do not blame me; for time brings everything to pass, and it burns away much of the memory of us men from the flow of the seasons.

<summary>This page contains the famous preface to Photius's "Bibliotheca," a letter to his brother Tarasius explaining that the following summaries of 225 books were compiled at Tarasius's request while Photius was departing on a diplomatic mission.</summary>
<keywords>Photius, Tarasius, Bibliotheca, Constantinople, Byzantine literature, embassy, manuscript preface, 9th century</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the summaries of theological and ethical treatises from the "Library" of Photius. Having introduced the diplomatic context and the work of Eulogius on the previous page, the text now transitions into a series of ethical exhortations and philosophical reflections on the nature of the soul, education, and the path to divine virtue.</meta>

...to keep themselves beyond the reach of regret; but indeed, persuasion is not profitable among those with whom one should not be joined. One might easily be able to restrain the young by adding more to those who are doing good according to their ability. But someone thinking otherwise might introduce **education**—and by education I mean not only that of the soul but also of the body—training them so that you never place women as guardians to keep the house <note>This likely refers to ancient social hierarchies or specific ethical precepts regarding the management of a household</note>. For they are not as some say, being both kindly and harmful; they are not always driven toward their neighbors, but these are the easy transitions toward doing evil, and one would not risk such wickedness. For you yourself are one of those inclined toward evil things; and all that corrupts our souls bleeds into pleasant things, clouding our daily concerns, whether they be their own fantasies or the unknown nature of the universe. Of these things, let the flight be toward God <note>original: πρὸ θεοῦ; literally "before God," implying a turning toward the divine</note> before all else; for God has pried open <note>original: ἀναμόχλευσε; a vivid verb meaning to lever or prize open, suggesting a divine unlocking of the soul</note>, perhaps not just the living parts of the naked body, but it is the nature of things to transform the outflow of the soul. 

And having touched upon the body or much of its simplicity, one tries, as if in the underworld, to lead him into battle pure, to defend the one who welcomes him without confusion through the things they said. He caused the heart to receive it, and he has succeeded in his hopes. For if such a man is blessed, it is a new work for the heart, and the wicked man is kept from doing worse things. (For he could not restore him because of this, nor can he be set on fire, unless he forces those acting wickedly in the soul to be put to shame. Nor could the soul, having taken away what belongs to itself, go out from its external affairs in a fitting manner.) 

It is harmonized, at least, and seeks a friend in its middle nature during the life of youth. They never broke down toward these things and they give leisure to **Reason** <note>original: λόγῳ; Logos, referring to both speech and the rational principle</note>, the soul possessing them completely. And those who say a prayerful spirit has settled upon it, he exhorts them against anger, fears, and griefs. At any rate, the corruption of the soul is put to rest through **stillness** <note>original: ἡσυχίας; *hesychia*, a technical term for inner quietude and contemplative silence</note>, and the excesses arising from it would suffice for the holy man, having sacrificed to God with a fear no longer fearful. 

That which is small is permitted to those who flee, who are not even just toward the worse; a victory song for the gain of both. As before the anger of external things, one must wisely take care of **discipline** <note>original: ἀσκήσεως; *askesis*, referring to the systematic training of the soul and body</note>. And discipline is for each of the others a constant occupation with one’s own affairs. Blessed **prudence** <note>original: φρόνησις; *phronesis*, or practical wisdom</note>, then, is the repentance always left to the soul. Just as if around horns, let us flee from oaths and the insulting memories of the rotten. But that which shines through when the sun is setting leads toward better things. For he who has not clothed his prayers in his present self, and a light for those so as not to weep for having committed sin, might be spoken of in fear through a metaphor for the soul, and she herself has sent that light.

<column-break/>

...granting favors; just as the powers exist for the soul, and you may speak Greek perfectly in this age. May it not happen, but rather that some forms of beauty contribute to **symmetry** <note>Proportion and balance, highly valued in Greek ethics and aesthetics</note> before evil things. 

Afterward, calling into the older parts of the soul with experience; after that pleasure of the wicked and of those among them who persuade the perfect and their punishment—which is more the nature of the soul to be such. For the **Intellect** <note>original: νοῦς; *nous*, the highest faculty of the mind</note> specifically borrowed from **Faith** <note>original: πίστεως; *pistis*</note>. No one was ever so inescapably not wicked and different while standing in abundance, but concerning his own affairs, he blesses the "heat-eater" <note>This is an unusual term, possibly referring to one consumed by passions or a specific ascetic reference</note> for all; most soft and reasonable and spiritual and gentle. 

And these things themselves are overtaken by the forgetfulness of nature, unless they should flee toward the whole, unless toward the movement of those things, the souls being dragged down. Relaxing toward those who flee it, their earth-bound zeal <note>original: γεωπαθῆ; passions or sufferings rooted in material, earthly existence</note> breathes again toward the eternal goods of the gods; they fulfill those who participate in them. And let these things be from those sources. 

It is worthy, therefore, both for **prudence** and all other forms of knowledge for souls under just laws, and for those who take care for prayers, coming under the noble man in nakedness. But a bad reputation concerning the gods is contrary to the glory of God. For these things are sufficient for those who happen upon them; even if those things which are just for all actions are not given. And those who are not even beautiful because of what power they loved to give—such as the cheapness of that intermediate **way of life** <note>original: πολιτείας; *politeia*, referring to one's conduct within a community or a "citizenship" of the soul</note>. On the one hand, by not turning away the things of the impious, and by prudence, the one who is entirely unlearned in display stands up for his own, the piety of houses and as if from... 

Of what good is that, the appropriate sacrifice for religious worship toward the divine? On the one hand, he reasonably dissolved the laurel of **temperance** <note>original: σωφροσύνης; *sophrosyne*, the virtue of moderation and self-control</note> into the moderation of living; and he masters his own temperate actions. For he thinks it possible only for the most worthy to be wise in a virtuous way; it shone forth even according to the dealings with males. Every nature of men, because not only is the proper living of the soul a piece of good fortune for him, but also his meditation and how he might be in good education and in season for the wicked man, for which reason it is for souls. He is beloved because of the instruction toward the temperance of the soul. Of those things called and of those in the river through each other, brought of the noble qualities into the whole, either only or most of them, or by the life-giving spirit of these toward the complete and the nature of the soul to be wise concerning the things manifest from there. 

A useful one; but doing this toward their own, with an effective mind in the permanence of virtue in the **way of life according to God**. Gentle and most soft, in the positions of their very souls.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on ethical discipline and the education of the soul. # On the Conduct of Life and the Soul

### The Image of the Virtuous Man

Each person is such; great were the errors men committed according to their reputation, <note>original: δόξαν; can mean both 'glory' and 'reputation'</note> avoiding the accusations and slanders against the soul, and everywhere providing themselves as likenesses of common things, just as **painters** do. While they look toward the conspicuous parts of life, they share among themselves the path, the study, and the zeal for these things, being ambitious in this way. They also demonstrate themselves to all serious people <note>original: σπουδαιοτάτοις; referring to those who are earnest or excellent in virtue</note> in all things that are fitting and proper. Therefore, they invite some not to let others rule over them, or they dine with them just as they would with those who are about to approach them, making them their own through their disposition, bringing rest to all through **benevolence**.

While they go about their lives, they show to their kin, to strangers, and to their fatherland that zeal alone exists, and not cowardice; or rather, the impulse of the soul lies within their own passions. They blush <note>original: φοινικόντες; literally 'turning crimson,' a sign of modesty or shame</note> at these things, fearing defeat or the reputation that comes to them from such things. Thus, they are most alone when they pay attention to those equal to them in concerns, and especially when they converse. They do not set out to teach the simple <note>original: ἁπλοῖς; the unlearned or plain-minded</note> when they are being educated themselves, but rather those who love learning and are serious about such matters. For this reason, they drive men out or shift their zeal toward other things, and they arrange themselves for those with a mind set on the **noble**. Indeed, the zeal of all is a serious thing.

Leading the life of an elder, they make their requests to God in **silence**. But also, after these things, they are without ambition; I do not speak of those who merely arrange these things or only show mercy, nor should those with them become subject to desire. For then they define education as a great thing, a catalog of sorts. He himself, learning in all things, also demonstrates the murderous nature <note>original: φονικόν; likely a metaphor for the 'killing' of the passions</note> of what was said. We hide those who are taught by another, just as they always await only the trivial things of some. They were hidden by him as a voice spoken of the people. But the **Great Law** of the voice is directed toward these things. Just as one flees from the hearing of those who clap <note>original: κροτούντων; referring to public applause or noisy approval</note>, let it be neither burdensome nor yet something that belongs only to the intellect. But after examining it further—as force commands him—so too the lover of learning <term>philologon: someone who loves words, reason, and study</term> keeps his speech well-prepared. And if again in conversations they do not have power over many, it is because of the well-tempered nature of their movement, leading a more quiet **education** that is carried everywhere upon them. They consider themselves praised through **humility**, and thus the whole of it is a familiarity with **philosophy**.

Many are those who choose especially your ambitious life; but there is also this: not to possess all his wisdom in an ecstatic state, but as has been previously understood, by becoming a serious man. He lacked for himself each part of **justice**, just as it is in and of itself...

<column-break/>

...from high things to humble ones, and even if he meditates on his head, they jump toward the things below. Lying down in his mind, he who not only holds the **inner world**, but also by command or by the order of the world, or he himself, performs this practice toward them. All things appear spontaneously; they share these with us and our most encompassing struggle. Such are the lives. And from many of them, he teaches some; and again, from those who shared the desert. And **salvation** comes through one's own private affairs, as the form of life commanded. 

Let me not give you something harsh; may it be yours as if to show a proverb by examining it. When the harsh thing comes to us, it strikes us and the righteous flesh. But may the **tongue** never pursue the man, for they called it so in the construction of desire. For they welcome lies as if they were precious; perhaps we do not know it, but only suspect it. But **education** by strangers is concerned with certain changes and the wanderings of those very people; they stumble, but we must appear well-ordered in what concerns us, being moved toward the **truth of souls**.

It is hypothesized that this is both perfectly known and entirely fitting for the **monk**; and for all of them, the sign of the teachers' way also guards us. From many writings and the images of his body that have appeared, each person's relationship to them is the necessary one within the body through its adornments. I shall allow it to provide for him that he always appears noble. But there is an exhortation to be **pious** <note>original: εὐλαβέσθαι; to hold in holy awe or reverence</note>, to try to empower and to join us. And if they are serious in their anger, they will not possess it, but being persuaded by one who meditates beforehand and by **confessing to the conscience**, many things are separated from their origins. To some, after the inscriptions, they wish to be familiar with their own kind, but those who are familiar with us appear everywhere.

**Prayer** is our own creation in **patience**. By giving as a submission, this is destined to happen: our prayers. We were reverent toward those who received us and toward our own correction, which you should accept with an additional offering, either now or after these things have been handed down. Out of this **love**, let them be serious for God, and at the same time, let them remember the words written as punishers. Every action according to the mind shows toward what things you will all be useful, so that the things given by God might not be hidden from you as you follow the lion of the lifestyle and the practice. He commands to cut through the daily affairs and at the same time to cry out for what is to come, so that...

# On Internal Discipline and the Spirit

...idling in fantasies, for he directs himself passionately toward those things that approach him. <margin>someone</margin> Therefore, he sees death before others, for as the same author says, it is in such an order of images. <margin>AL</margin> And if the soul almost never departs from the body, neither the one who imagines nor the one who is spiritually wronged [is far from God], for God reaches into every heart. But he possesses within himself every desirable thing. And through this, he shall stand apart from danger, seeing himself stripped of the desire for things pertaining to the body. And he directs the rhythmic harmony of his passion toward the love of God, without commanding anything. [He is under] guard, as long as the meditations of the living and the priests [continue]; God is before all things and does everything else for the sake of the knowledge of beings, even the removal of wealth. To those who pray and do not possess the goods of God, the springs of nature are not the source of the poor man's greed. He makes himself a fantasy to himself, should they happen upon it, putting to sleep any of the desirable things. This is according to nature <margin>of</margin> for those who meditate, making what is best into a meditation on fantasy—having thus somehow regulated me out of madness. And this meditation is divine and protective, where life meets them in spirit, body, and blood. 

But if anyone has discerned among bodies, there is an indwelling for those lying there, and they place this body in their own [places], <margin>as</margin> and it was made manifest; but the kinship according to the body leads back again to the beginning of nature, from the spirit into the spirit, which is the whole body. But God is the spirit, thus guiding like a rod <margin>as</margin> toward that meditation with the power of the perfect soul. To bring the [quality] of life to the soul. For before this, <margin>and</margin> His spirit was over all. He is a youth, and even from the veins those who are foolish have been lowered. <margin>of</margin> Nor even when he departs. Being mocked in the form of a preconception according to what is set forth <margin>to those</margin> in time. And God is the creator to these same people (but having been enlightened). Since God is life-giving and fertile, and how shall it not be fulfilled before the world, nor of the spiritual things? But others, let them be separated from the works of the body, and those present having flowed away, likewise of the spirits lying under those things, <margin>of</margin> the spirit of those who practice protection, such as is the whole God-inspired spirit to those who have power; for this spirit will not grow weary, being thus driven out by the passion within itself, how the divine [author] says it has been transformed again toward the divine image.

---

-> Epigram of Saint Gregory the Theologian for the Great Basil <-

The herald of repentance and of the law and of fear is the great teacher of the fathers. I see all his works, he says, as common to all under the sun; for all of the Great Basil is a <note>Gregory and Basil were the "Cappadocian Fathers," famous for their deep friendship and theological collaboration.</note> debt of gratitude to God because of the benefit which he himself provided to each person.

<column-break/>

(Having written these things thus concerning those possessed by demons, they did not fashion the form of wickedness in this way) beyond the paths and their fear, but a form that is put to shame. For it is not according to their nature that <margin>AL</margin> repentance is enslaved to that [nature]. Before our very birth. Since he was there where she might be, for do not spare him alone. But giving the whole matter, and to turn back toward him and in a manner <margin>to those</margin> to purify yourself as a man from misfortunes, by the spirit. Fitting to nature and to high knowledge. <margin>L</margin> Since as many things as come to each of us upon the same [path] of spiritual desires. All things simple receive the [inclinations] toward themselves and their own enjoyment. Finally, for most people, it grows around the meditations of the gods. <margin>the</margin> But the fantasies having been conquered, the soul is voluntary. And having renounced the life of the evil one among things that happen and calling out his ways. And according to its own matter, which the parent of the race <margin>the</margin> wove together with it. And this he thus makes a meditation for God, not even relaxing the zeal of the one before her. 

Therefore, the guards are inspired by breath, for the tongue and the prayer and every power of the spirit, being meditated upon, <margin>the</margin> is the cause of this toward God, from whom all things come and who is Himself the source. Therefore, indeed, the things of God according to the purely [spiritual] man, thus he dedicates all his own in meditation, and we excel in our race because of God. But if anyone is also watchful, having settled the passions of those evil ones and the other movements within her, and [having settled] to meditate on her own birth with the casting out of darkness by the light of piety with <margin>the</margin> image-making, and reverence toward that blessedness so that he might be deemed worthy of paternal honor; and because after letting go of the things from which there is no proof, [they show] that they will fail in their nature. To seal through the spirit, <margin>the</margin> so that before the second and then spiritual resurrection, he might restore it again to the province.

---

> For this [soul] I [seek] unceasingly from your all-holy soul.

---

A little while before our death it is possible, and it may appear to the love of God that it lies there—[free] of passions and not according to what is not of God. But according to himself in the life in God. (For he who has been separated from the things of the body <margin>body</margin> rises) all things in the one lying there, and he calls this a body. And knowledge is carried along and the remaining <margin>of</margin> main point, from where the substance [comes], not from [the earth], but indeed by a descent before the foundation. But in these activities <margin>of</margin> and this changes us, just as if we were base and vile and the weakest of this, not of heaven nor of the beginning of nature in power and the exit of corruption. And the present [judgment] of the meditation of God has been completed, <margin>of</margin> and later toward the meditation of piety, he went out with us again toward those terrible things, <margin>the</margin> being watchful even before the body, and it will not suffice through mercy and compassions; those things indeed came through, the source healed everything in the spirit before all the churches. Both after the things according to himself, as someone said himself, and those his own things, finally after life, the sacred and blessed things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on spiritual discipline, shifting from the control of mental fantasies to a commentary on the nature of the "assembly" (synagogue) versus the Church, and the struggle against "subterranean" or hidden passions. It appears to be a commentary on the works of Gregory of Nazianzus, specifically touching upon the contrast between servitude and freedom.</meta>

<margin>4</margin>
The assembly <note>original: "Ἡ συναγωγή" – while this can mean a Jewish synagogue, in this patristic context it often refers to the legalistic "assembly" of the old law in contrast to the grace of the Church</note> is not from the same God, and those who belong to it act proportionally; it is as if one were to tread upon a stone with great care, yet would not desire the flow of springs; nor will he be moved from the state of servants. And you must arrive like those who have been brought back from servitude, like a father in a house who has been unjustly held down by evils. But to these very people, natural and good things will appear. Servitude, on the one hand, belongs to brothers who envy small things; and these are counted among those who have been set free, and those who oppose the one being guarded within the Church. For they say that nothing comes back to them again, for they claim that things have reached their fulfillment, even those things existing now.

Because of this, the subterranean <term>rage</term> <note>original: "κατώρυχον μένος" – a poetic term for deep-seated, hidden, or "buried" passion or anger</note> of those who are with us once again exists. Out of shame for what is said, some things are assigned to blame; at another time, those things which reasonably belong to the hands or to our body are used as a pretext. And nothing is directed toward the thing that was shamed, so that the things happening to them all do not involve a "decorative folly" <note>likely referring to vanity or outward show</note> even after their wandering. Rather, the judgment is guarded, just as with those who do not have the means to spend on all the same things as the many. And thus again, the angelic and divine things become more fervent and more ambitious.

O Psalmist <note>original: "Ψάλτα" – likely addressing the author of the psalms or the singer of the hymn being commented upon</note> again, the shamed middle part—the things that are one's own—or those things perhaps as they were before the time of war, are given so that they might see, therefore, through the ears of those who hear. Perhaps it is so that even those within—to whom the enemies [look]—might see the guards working as living beings. These things belong to those most philanthropic and pious ones of all who have been sent forth. Since they are alone, must they not differ greatly in soul because they have departed into faith? For they do not even deem the danger worthy of every bitter use against all enemies again. For after them comes a defense, and not even in an ordinary moment is there a lack of care for one's own affairs. Not that the prayer for good things has been fulfilled for them as a form of healing; for they do not flee from their own piety. But even if the giver pursues a portion of their affairs, and if indeed the things he possesses regarding grace are magnificent and easier, it is still necessary to stand and attain it for oneself, even through blood, just as it was before. These are terrible things when combined with labor; one must search out these things and the members of those who watch, especially when the time of rest ceases. It is as if the father is caring for the good through prayer.

And here, he turns to the care of the virtues and the care of the "aromatics" <note>likely a metaphor for the "sweet-smelling" fruits of virtue or incense used in prayer</note>; but he comes first to such matters.

<summary>This page contains a theological commentary contrasting the "servitude" of the old assembly with the freedom of the Church, while analyzing the "subterranean rage" of human passion and the necessity of spiritual labor and prayer.</summary>

Indeed, these things require fame; for you love him for all his virtues, and it is right that you do so; for through the world’s order, we are led toward you. <margin>Notes on the nature of divine radiance and the soul's ascent.</margin>
If wisdom <note>original: "phronesis" — practical wisdom or prudence</note> is a thing to be prayed for by all, then he will also reach out, as I do, for such things. For what kind of divine loves, reachings-forth, and longings will you receive? Looking upon the rays from that place, or rather the outflows. As if someone might think the antiquity of things comes from there, but instead he is filled with such things; himself a symbol of return; and away from mere wonder-working, he who travels the sacred road brings desire to the soul; a good for him and for his ambition, or rather for God himself. Through him, the things divided there are softened, as are the elevations of each <unclear>soul</unclear>; for that man is formed from secret <unclear>light</unclear> and beautiful things. He is not imagined from some ancient gods and sacred rites in a corner, which would keep you and the pure things of virtue apart; but the world is full of those things spoken from that place. Thus for us, the whole seems to resemble him; and even that there is much light there, reaching toward a great abundance; the time allotted to them by providence <note>original: "pronoia"</note>; and among such things, it always <unclear>remains</unclear> for those born among them.

<margin>A warning against the "contrary" or malicious spirits that lead the soul astray.</margin>
But now it seems to me that we should also consider the things of the contraries; both the spiritual beings and the most wicked things, having left behind <insert>their</insert> divine and more honorable aspects, to revile or cast away the glory of the same; and to call them a lie and a conceit. For what kind of worldly passions are they, or does everyone stand aloof? But God, through what has happened, remains in all things, for not even those things most beneficial to the soul are lost; but from them we are carried to God. But even those things that are not such, in all judgments, are crowned; so that both might be manifest to God himself as being always separate; and his significance reveals the souls and those that follow to the complete and all-working power of this present life. <margin>Commentary on the "dances of God" and the harmony of the virtues.</margin>
A blessed thing and to be prayed for by all who are of sound mind, since it works the good nature of the soul through all things. It is nothing other than the fact that both the spiritual beings and the divine things—or rather the portion of God—participate in these things and share in them. Since such things are for all of us: both a hope for the future, where all things abound in a portion of divine <unclear>protection</unclear>, a thing to be prayed for everywhere and a foundation for them, as much as all thought or the apostasies; and how it is for those toward it. And it is possible that each form of the soul will receive in its movements and the dances of God and his own voice, a part of music. Of these, is one complete? And the path of the virtues is for all; and of the sacred movements; whoever he may be, or rather the things according to the movements and through the power over them, thus also the souls are separated. Those disposed with it; he increased them and for the many they are just and good; but she herself, surely not in the same way; and those who are nothing, or according to such as these; credibility of the exposition.

<margin>On the "divine nobility" (theia eugeneia) as a gift of the spirit.</margin>
Concerning the spirit <note>original: "pneuma"</note> and divine nobility, it is equally firm for all; and those things referred back to the Mind <note>original: "Nous"</note>; it is and always is the same by nature. For all human things, both those toward him and those toward God himself, had a rising up from her; and bodies for them according to us or for his fathers; for the perfect disciples. And the divine things are beautiful for all of them; and in words, the virtues of the soul; grace; and for all, the things of judgment; and the essences over them; and for these, the same things are prepared for such a person. Because of this, both the repositories and the powers of nature; those things according to the more divine and the things equally for all in the present; always common to all and to those who are quick to learn.

<margin>The "Hierophant of Life" — one who initiates others into the sacred mysteries of living well.</margin>
Since by this word of the virtues, and also by the spirit; and by God in every way, they say to everyone; and the present starting-points, of the things proclaimed, for they are toward the mindset. And he says what is right among those where he is a friend; for thus all wisdom is to be taken up further by the word and the things according to the Mind, this indeed because of wisdom. For we know beautiful things by the same word, nor indeed is a vision necessary for all methods; either toward the divine or these themselves, but no longer the things of the spirits themselves; but also those toward the world, nor shall we be persuaded by those who move all divine things by the present movement. And again the passions upon him and those in the movements and wisdom and all such things; so that those who divide the movements [into] as many thoughts as they can. <meta>This page transitions from the general pursuit of wisdom and divine "rays" discussed on the previous page to the practical application of these virtues within a community. It moves from the abstract "First Good" to the concrete "measure" of daily life, emphasizing charity to the poor and the struggle between spiritual mindset and bodily impulses.</meta>

<margin>1</margin>
As for us, in managing our own affairs, we live according to the measure <note>original: "metron" — the standard of moderation or proportion</note> that we have allotted for our generation, and we fulfill the needs of the brothers; and not only that, but also the needs of the poor. We define these things within our own boundaries; for I do not boast in the affairs of others, nor do I attempt to push them aside; and so it is with all the earth in the inhabited world. May we never remain merely human anywhere on earth, nor let the strength of idleness prevail, for those who look toward these and similar things. To these people, such things are not so much a matter of conscience, yet nonetheless, the affairs of those who sell everything are considered, just like the affairs of those who act. If we look at each thing in succession, we are content to have peace and concord; let us take nothing from anyone. And toward one another, from which source their piety <note>original: "eusebeia" — a central term meaning godly devotion or religious duty</note> and the reverence of the sensory organ around us are especially blended, as all that is precious and glorious in life is from God. But regarding the things mentioned: they are not as numerous as sand, as much as the causes of piety toward God. And if no one else remains, our own water shall be of the beginning, not for the sake of thirst, nor for what comes before it. Since for everyone and what follows, it is necessary to set down as many things as are accompanied by reverence, good order, and great gentleness; we contribute from these things to the customary habits, choices, and administrations. So that we are not merely satisfied with the same things that reach the many, even the things before the discourse shall be ours from you; and for this reason, let these words of ours be searched out, so that your affairs may be handled piously according to our ability.

<margin>2</margin>
**T**hey devise many wicked things; those who choose evil strive to drag others toward it in every instance. For this reason, not even considering what is for each other's mutual benefit, they humbly measure out their order with us. But there, they say, is how one lives temperately, whence he says: "The man is perfect <note>original: "aner teleios" — likely a reference to James 3:2, meaning someone spiritually mature or complete</note> who speaks." A man for whom the measure from us is on one hand directed toward dangers, and those things are cut short in our heart, or perhaps craftily. Such a mindset <note>original: "gnome" — intention or judgment</note> is their own sting toward evil and dangerous things. For it is with caution and through poetic action that we are in a good state in this manner. Furthermore, the truth regarding all brotherly things is this: that it does not even lead to things against a woman; and such a person would not only persuade a woman in this way, but also avoid the suspicions and evils toward her. For if nothing has occurred in wicked works, it is noted in these signs; but they also terrify and show mercy upon all. That which belongs to God, just as with the saints and those set before us, concerns the things of the body. And for this reason, one must not fear your own self within yourselves. He spoke the fitting voice, as if in the judgments of the ancient parent <note>This likely refers to Adam in the Garden of Eden</note>, toward God; he was the first to hear this. And things of fear are as providers to the many; both bodies and spirits (and the rest in order). Just as the wicked are murderers and bloodthirsty toward all things, being held fast by their own particular evil; so are the things toward justice and what follows. But above all things is love <note>original: "agape" — selfless, divine love</note>, the bringing together of one's own self for everyone, so that toward the pathways of the poor, there is great communion with the commandments of the Lord. They flee the natural mindset <note>original: "phronema" — spirit or way of thinking</note>, fearing sins but not feeling shame.

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
Because the lamps are from heaven, from the providence of God; and these same are the causes of the wicked. For he did not have the grace of God from the things set before him; for neither in shining attentively and thoughtlessly, is there great and total virtue <note>original: "arete"</note>. For in this way, those who handle divine and written things do so not without some labor and diligence. For here, the mindset of the soul is through love for God, not through wicked bodies and affairs. One must unceasingly guard the path toward orthodoxy and doctrines; and the things contained in them, or even the ailments of the body among the pious. But that which is in the spirit is through grace, which He gave to the prophets of souls: the total sympathy of the spirit and the doing of good for the many. Not only the things of the soul, lest they ever turn away from piety toward God, for in this way the members of wickedness are surpassed; thus, at any rate, even inflammation and the things that go with it. Thus also the spirit of virtue, just as the body, through love toward God and toward the poor, shall (as he says) certainly be. That which concerns the spirit and that which is through actions; that which is in the spirit, the thought and power of the spirit. And so it is with the things of temperance. For those who do such things piously have God as merciful. Because even every power of the wicked is made strong from the strength of the virtues; and the things of the mind are strong, even if they only look toward God. And one should show mercy to the virtue toward God and to the hungry and the poor; for it is a law. This is so that the things of the body may be guarded, as well as the things toward the strength of the spirit; and so it is with the affairs of the poor; and toward the things of the flesh performed according to piety; and the body. And for the pious, not only toward the body, but also toward the weakness of the body. For either the soul manages things according to the spirit and the things before the body, or the flesh does so because of nature. For in this way, wicked and evil things lead toward wickedness. For not even in these things are they made familiar toward the body in the present time, for it is not the benefit of the soul, but the things toward the poor. Those other things lead astray. And generally, the things especially concerning themselves, and those who have more faith toward God. Rightly also the mindset; and that their own affairs toward God be unwavering. For either such things lead toward illness; for such a thing must also be just. For that person and such things—the nakedness and the body toward administrations and wicked things—not the things for the body. For indeed, the body and the blood of the spirit are toward God; and piety toward God, in the things that follow. And the things of God are not before the goal; both the things said and the things with them; and the things toward the judgment; and giving rest to the soul; and the things of piety. For he who is in all these, is also before the others; and the things toward the soul; and thus to have the things toward the truth. For it appears that some things are soul-destroying, while others are saving; and some are this way and some that, but to the righteous God and the Holy Spirit belongs all faith and love and virtue toward God. And so is the matter of the poor; and before many of the good things in life, both those who are for the sake of virtue and those who are toward God; and toward the glory of God, and the things according to God, and the things before the administrations and what follows.

+ These things, therefore, before the discourse, have been made known through themselves and before the deeds.

<note>Glossary of key terms used in this passage: Mindset/Spirit, The Poor, Providence, Piety, Virtue, Spirit, Love.</note>

It emphasizes that true virtue and "orthodoxy" are maintained through love for God and practical acts of mercy.</summary>

<page-num>42</page-num>

...what it is. This is most clearly seen in the heavens; and through it, He distributes to all; and through this very power, He also holds existing things together; and there is nothing that does not participate in His power. One might call this "spirit" <note>original: "pneuma" — meaning breath, wind, or spirit</note>, that subtle, light-like, and ever-moving nature, which is suited both to the composition of the whole universe and to the individual essence of each being, and supplies its life-giving power to all. For heaven and earth, and everything between them, all depend upon the divine power. And this is the very sun of light, passing through all things, and supplying its life-giving power to all, to which the rest of the stars also provide what is needed.

<margin>How it should be understood</margin>
Since, therefore, the Divine is thus harmonized with all things, for this reason the birth of light also occurs—not as something else among existing things, but as the divine fire itself, and the life-giving spirit. The power seen in all existing things is light and life and whatever good one might name. As for how light came to be, or how the sun and the rest of the stars were made, it is not useful to detail for the present subject. But that the divine power is harmonized with all, and gives life to all things, and passes through all, and nothing is devoid of the divine power, has already been sufficiently demonstrated in what was said before. For heaven and earth, and everything between them—some through their essence, others through their activity—all depend upon the divine power. And this is the very sun of light, passing through all things, and supplying its life-giving power to all.

...indeed. These elements <term>stoicheia<note>The four basic components of the physical world: earth, air, fire, and water</note></term> themselves, through their own means, are harmonized for the composition of all things. For he says that all things are bound by the spirit; some things are bound to the whole, while the heaven is bound to itself, because it has nothing outside it to which it could be joined. By the spirit, it is harmonized with itself, and with all the elements, and these with themselves and with the whole. Through the power directed toward the whole, it is harmonized both with itself and with the nature of each individual part. <gloss>73</gloss> He speaks of the things of the spirit, not because it is something divine and immaterial, but because it is more subtle than the others, having a nature like that of a spirit or air; it holds within itself the cohesive power of beings, and by this, all things are bound together. <gloss>74</gloss> Therefore, when God says, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," He named the extremities of the whole; and by "heaven" and "earth," He included everything in between. <gloss>75</gloss> Now, the heaven, because of its more subtle nature, draws closer to the Divine, while the earth is held at the furthest points, placed like a foundation <note>original: "pythmēn" — meaning the bottom or base of a vessel</note> beneath the cosmos. Since, therefore, the extremities are harmonized with one another by the spiritual power, the communion of these things with one another occurs through the middle parts; so that the things of the earth are distributed to the heaven, and the things of the heaven to the earth, through those parts that are naturally suited to one another. <gloss>76</gloss> And thus the Divine is in all things, and passes through all, and supplies its life-giving power to all, and nothing among existing things is devoid of the divine power. Since, therefore, the Divine is thus harmonized with all things, for this reason the birth of light also occurs—not as something else among existing things, but as the divine fire itself, and the life-giving spirit. The power seen in all existing things is light and life and whatever good one might name. <gloss>77</gloss> As for how light came to be, or how the sun and the rest of the stars were made, it is not useful to detail for the present subject. But that the divine power is harmonized with all, and gives life to all things, and passes through all, and nothing is devoid of the divine power, has already been sufficiently demonstrated in what was said before. <gloss>78</gloss> For heaven and earth, and everything between them—some through their essence, others through their activity—all depend upon the divine power. And this is the very sun of light, passing through all things, and supplying its life-giving power to all, to which the rest of the stars also provide what is needed.

...with gladness their minds; to these He grants glory and exultation. They say, therefore, that there is a path for us toward an immaterial life <note>original: "aylon bion." ### <unclear>From the</unclear> <unclear>Homilies on the</unclear> <unclear>Apostles</unclear>, Homily 25: <unclear>by Chrysostom</unclear> <note>original: "ὑπὸ χρυσοστόμου." Referring to John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), the Archbishop of Constantinople known for his powerful preaching.</note>
One, three <unclear>ethereal</unclear> names <note>Likely a reference to the Holy Trinity—one God in three persons—described here with the "ethereal" or heavenly quality mentioned on the previous page.</note> or those of the greatest <unclear>champion</unclear>.

If we are called daily to the palace by the summons of the king, <unclear>purifying</unclear> ourselves immediately, then angels stand by us, having set us free. And if it were a terrible thing, should we say it is an honor to receive the king’s salvation, calling us to the court and convening us? Therefore, there is an equal mystery <term>mystery: 'mysterion' refers to a divine truth or a sacramental act that reveals God's grace</term> in what is happening. How is it both awesome and fearsome, and yet worthy of joy and more joy?

Do you wish to learn where there are no more tears? For how is this a proof of the greatest wisdom? Is it not like leaving a house, the soul having come to its own silencing and having been washed? The soul is released as if from some prison; it comes out as if from a battle.

For even that person says it surrounded him, so that we might be persuaded as to what it is. For just as the sun rises pure, so also the soul, having left the body with the boldness of glory, is bright and radiant. A king entering a city does not come with such great honor as a soul leaving the body and departing with angels. For if it should obtain these things, it is touched with amazement and rejoices, even after being held by the body.

<meta>This page continues the homily from folio 47, transitioning from the description of the soul’s departure to the proper way the living should mourn and assist the deceased. The author, John Chrysostom, argues that worldly wailing is useless, but almsgiving and prayer can provide actual relief to the soul of the departed.</meta>

How does it seem to you? Tell me, what does this fire signify? <note>original: "τί πῦρ θέλει"</note> Is it because you do this for a sinner? I wish you would weep for the sin itself; then I would not prevent the mourning. If only this were your purpose! But your grief is not for what is pitiable in an apostolic sense; it is not about the inner character, but about appearances. Paul wept for three years, <note>A reference to Acts 20:31, where St. Paul describes his tearful ministry in Ephesus.</note> day and night, over what was happening. This is the kind of mourning we need. When it is necessary, and when one is weeping, you speak of peace and diligence and attention; yet you were not sent for this, but to dig deep into the soul. 

Mourn for the sinner in silence. I have within me the tears that flow outward, and I have felt them. The greater the punishment such a person is liable for, the more we should lament for their soul’s destination. It is not only you who should mourn such a person, but the entire city and those everywhere. Perhaps, just as someone being led away to slaughter is a sight that makes everyone feel it is proper to help the sinner. But instead, external things have been turned upside down. This is not about appearances; it is a matter of philosophy <term>philosophy: 'philosophia' in this context refers to the Christian disciplined life and spiritual wisdom</term> and it contains much teaching. 

Regarding the sacred matters—or rather, the occasion—if we were to lament them truly, we would have corrected their lives. Just as there is a right time to apply medicines that prevent death, if you had lamented that death [of the soul] while they lived, you would have prevented it both for yourself and for the one who has died. But now, what is happening is an enigma. The Lord does not allow this to happen more than is fitting; it has been released. But for the one who has passed, it is better to act. Such a one is truly worthy of lamentation when they stand before the judgment seat <term>judgment seat: 'bema,' the tribunal of God</term> and hear the judgments. What matters these are for those who have stumbled! There, things are revealed—or rather, not only there, but even here. And if anyone happens to have an opportunity to help, it is beneficial if they promised it. What shall we say to friends? For such a person will be caught calling down judgment upon his own head. If only Paul were present, even he would not have been enough to cover the loss.

<column-break/>

Tell me, what should we do? Should we continue doing this in the house for twenty more years? It is not fitting for you to do these things; it will seem to everyone that the benefit comes from almsgiving. <note>original: "ἐλεημοσύνης ὄνησις"</note> This is the most urgent duty for all the living. Not a single sin is cast out by worldly grief, but rather by rejecting luxury, by avoiding greed, and by conquering sin and the devil. Should we then not mourn? Tell me! If there are trials, should I say all these things are wonders? For those who have gone astray, we should desire for their punishment to become milder. 

Let us offer prayers for them continuously; let us give alms. <term>alms: 'eleemosynas,' acts of charity or money given to the poor as a spiritual offering</term> Even if that person is unworthy, God will be moved by us. If Paul burned with concern for the Greeks, and others were helped, how much more will we be helped? This is what we must do: not by spending money out of habit, but out of knowledge. Give from wherever you wish. Offer oil, or rather, offer water. Do you not have alms to give? Is it not possible to receive? Even if you have gathered little, do you not have what was stripped from him? Even if it is for his sake, so that you may rescue him from that bitter storm <note>The "bitter storm" is a common metaphor for the pains of the afterlife or the judgment.</note> by standing up for him. 

The more sins he was responsible for, the more alms he needs. This is not just for such a person, but for everyone who lacks the strength to care for the many. For it is not the same for someone to act for himself as it is for others to act on his behalf. Thus, let us fill the void with our own honor. Let these not be merely "burial-around" gifts or "grave-persuaders," as they are called. This is for the one who is burning. Hear the need: every command made on his behalf before the Master and the supplications will give him everything from God. Even if he is not directly delighted by it, the benefit of the almsgiving still reaches him. This is because of God’s love for mankind. <note>original: "φιλανθρωπίας"</note> Remember how the widows stood around weeping; <note>Refers to Acts 9:39, where widows showed St. Peter the clothes Tabitha had made, leading to her being raised from the dead.</note> they did not just weep for the person...

<summary>John Chrysostom argues that worldly mourning for the dead is useless compared to the spiritual benefits of almsgiving and prayer, which can actually mitigate a soul's punishment. He uses the biblical example of the widows weeping for Tabitha to illustrate how charity moves God to mercy.</summary>
