# On Assistance for the Departed

...present; but also to persuade the one about to snatch them from death. Many have also benefited from the alms sent by others on their behalf; for even if the relief was not complete, they nevertheless found some consolation. For if this were not possible, how is it that infants are baptized? <note>Chrysostom uses infant baptism as a logical proof: if a child can receive the grace of baptism through the faith of parents, the dead can receive grace through the alms of the living.</note> At that moment, the child contributes nothing themselves, but the parents provide everything. Infants often enjoy these graces despite having brought nothing of their own to the act. Since God has sent us, how is it not possible for the one who gives to be of help? If there is no blame to be found, many gains might result. For many benefit not only from the wealth of the alms given, but also from the intention <term>intention: 'proairesis', the moral choice or purposeful heart of the giver</term> behind them. 

Let us be persuaded by the facts of the matter; for these traditions were not established at random or without careful examination. Rather, by following this path, you have something to trust in. The compassionate God will grant justice to the departed, for He does not appear to be contentious. This is what we ourselves should learn by grace. Let us be eager to have another person or a clear friend to do this for us—whether a wife or a friend. For just as they remember themselves, even if they reap only a small fruit, they are reaping something nonetheless. While wealth may provide a type of rest, it is so that all glory and gladness may be a solemn thing for those who have gone before, that they might enjoy this consolation. Take hold of these truths, for you yourself know this: that the one who does such things is surrounded by friends, a wife, and children. It was not said in vain that offerings <term>offerings: 'prosphora', specifically the bread and wine brought for the Eucharist</term> are made on behalf of the departed. It was not said in vain that there are supplications; it was not said in vain that there are alms. All these things were ordained by the Spirit. Therefore, see how he wishes to help in every way. Does that person benefit? Indeed, it will benefit him. For even a burden of wealth, when added wrongly, creates spiritual poverty; but this creates salvation for both you and him. Regarding almsgiving, one is the cause of the other; do not doubt what fruit it will bear...

<column-break/>

...something good. The priest does not simply cry out prayers for those who have fallen asleep <note>original: "κεκοιμημένων", a common Christian term for the deceased, implying they will wake again</note> and for the things being done by them. Consider how many things the deacon commands during the prayers, and the voice of those prayers. But consider especially that dreadful sacrifice <note>original: "τὸ θῦμα τὸ φρικτὸν", referring to the presence of Christ in the Eucharist</note>. With a multitude of thanksgivings, they bring forward everything that is fitting for the calling. 

Angels and archangels are present; the Son of God is present. Everyone stands there with such great awe. They stand there crying out for the goodwill of the servants—is it not through this that the fullness of what is done comes to pass? Do not think that these things, or the things offered for the Church, or the things offered for the priests, are done simply at random. After this, we believe that all these things are offered to the Spirit. To be called upon at that hour, even if one is a martyr—even if it is on behalf of martyrs—it is a great honor to be named while the Lord is present, while that most dreadful sacrifice <note>original: "τῆς φρικωδεστάτης θυσίας"</note> is being performed, and those ineffable mysteries are taking place. 

For just as when someone sits near the king, they can prevail in whatever they wish because the king grants favors according to the custom; so it is at that time. When the mysteries are set forth, it is the highest honor for everyone there to be deemed worthy of mention. For see, the dreadful mystery is then proclaimed: that God gave Himself for the whole world <note>original: "οἰκουμένη", the inhabited world</note>. Along with that miracle, you opportunely remind Him of those who have sinned. For just as earthly kings are honored not just on their birthdays, but those who are celebrated are also honored by their subjects—and they even release prisoners from their bonds because of the festive season, though once the season passes, one might no longer enjoy such a favor—so it is here. This is the time of the heavenly celebration. For as often as you eat this bread, you proclaim the Lord's death...

### After the prayer to Christ; and the Sovereign Hope of the faithful
It is fitting for Christians to know: what a Christian is, and how a Christian ought to live as a citizen; and regarding theology <term>theology: here used in the strict sense of the study of God’s inner life, rather than general religion</term>, to know the study of nature and the knowledge of the Godhead. Believe then, beloved, in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding <note>original: "ekporeuton"—the technical term for the Spirit's origin from the Father</note>. These persons <term>persons: 'hypostaseis', the individual realities of the Trinity as distinct from their shared essence</term> differ in themselves and from one another by their source and cause, and by the personhood according to which the begetting occurs. He has no "making" <note>meaning the Son is not a created thing</note>; for the whole essence <term>essence: 'ousia', the common divine nature shared by the Trinity</term> is through the Father, and the Spirit is the source from Him. According to each source, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but is bestowed upon the faithful through the Son. But they confess that this nature has its own distinct existence, and is nothing more than this procession. Regarding the Godhead, we confess to those who are obedient, as it has been said: it leads back to the source and the person. We believe in every essence through the Father, and again, a nature that is not like any other. There are five natures in general things, and in relation to the individual persons of the persons: the Godhead truly exists, beloved; as the nature takes form in them, it was known by...

<column-break/>

<margin>LL</margin>
...confesses the persons <note>original: "hypostaseis"</note> in the Godhead: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; three in person, but one in essence. For that which happens to be numbered manifests certain characteristics; for the one, the two, the three, and so forth, even the five and the rest, reveal the forms to all; names and numbers stand still. But reason <note>original: "logike"—logical or rational discourse</note> regarding the three persons, by its movement, sees the source as equal to the things generated by God. For the source is common, so that those who have been generated may receive the kingdom. In the "image" <note>likely referring to man being made in the image of God</note> this is naturally confessed, because of "Godhead and Godhead" <note>the repetition emphasizes the equality of the persons</note>. And if they were to posit the Divine and the Holy Creation, then the natural aspect of the Godhead and its activity <term>activity: 'energeia', the outward work of God in the world</term> applies to the rest. But if they should learn of a "holy malice," whenever it is the will of God, it makes things pure, just as it is the will of God. They see that the faith which was worked out for salvation by the Holy Fathers came from unknown causes. Regarding spiritual discourse, these things must again be directed toward the spiritual; they have become spiritual. One must first know those things which are common and those which are most unique. The "common" things of the Godhead regarding the Economy <term>Economy: 'oikonomia', God’s plan for the salvation of the world</term> is the Word: there is one and the same power, the power of the source. And this is known in the Father and in the Son. He shares in the nature of His Godhead, insofar as He shares in the source of God; and He shares in the source of the source, which is His goodness, insofar as He is also holy and perfect. How it is said to "arrive" and how it is addressed, you shall hear and know, with a love for the truth. There is one source and the grace of the source: one will, one wisdom, one power. We pray in common, and it is not received differently by the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the nature of each—that of the Father and that of the Son—is the characteristic of nature, and is known as a characteristic in each. All personhood is great and good through the blessing of the Father. For all is first of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit confessedly; and the name of "God" is called common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But that which they hold in themselves as a source are not common names, but are unique to each...

<meta>This page continues the technical theological definitions begun on the previous page. The text focuses on defining the "Divine Nature" versus "Divine Persons" using traditional Patristic vocabulary and the famous analogy of Peter and Paul to explain how three distinct Persons can share one single Essence.</meta>

...beyond understanding <note>original: "hyper noun"—literally above the mind or intellect</note>. For He is not called "Son" in a worldly sense, nor is He called "Father" in a worldly sense; rather, all things from God are brought forth in this way. For when "God" is named, I speak of the **divine subsistence** <term>subsistence: 'hypostasis', the individual reality of a person in the Trinity as distinct from their shared nature</term>, or of a certain Person, both their unique property and their nature. 

The divine nature—from which I said "to nourish" <note>likely a folk etymology connecting 'Theos' (God) with 'theein' (to run) or a similar root relating to providence</note>—is what the study of nature has set apart for us. For I say to all that **essence** and **nature** are the same thing, while **subsistence** <gloss>hypostasis</gloss> refers to the individual. This is a hundredfold distinction. But regarding the subsistence: those who properly value the Persons signify the essence and the nature as that which "God" means.

What then is God? An uncreated, bodiless essence. He is therefore also **incomprehensible**. An unbound beauty. An invisible greatness. An unadorned nature. An unthinkable glory. Every good thing. A spiritual light. For those who have been created, He is an inexhaustible glory. An unchangeable essence. A personal character <note>original: "charakter enypostatos"—referring to the specific expression of a person's existence</note> within the Source. The source of life, wisdom, and goodness; and from Him, it is clear and bright. The beginning of blessedness. Undefiled light. The Only-Begotten Son and the image of the Father, who is the Sun. The light is the ray of the sun; the heat of the ray is the **All-Holy Spirit**.

Yet all of this is fire. But it is also light. To us, fire is that which burns, but the All-Holy Spirit is [different]. And so the Father is the Father of the Son, and he spoke of these essentialities before all things. There is the fire which is known [to us], and the fire which must be understood beforehand. And since divine things exist in three subsistences of the Godhead—in nature, in form, and together—one must contract the subsistence and the Person into the same thing, just as Scripture marks a certain light as common to the essence. 

For the **subsistence** <gloss>hypostasis</gloss> is the **Person** <gloss>prosopon</gloss>. It is that which marks out what is unique to each. Just as for us, for instance: **Peter and Paul** are of one and the same nature <note>the common nature of "humanity"</note>. However, the subsistence <gloss>hypostasis</gloss> is the difference between them, while the nature is their communion with one another. For this reason, it is necessary to declare these things, or toward this <unclear>unclear</unclear>...

<summary>This page defines the technical differences between 'essence' (shared nature) and 'hypostasis' (individual personhood) within the Trinity. It uses the light/ray/heat and Peter/Paul analogies to explain how God can be both Three and One.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from abstract theological definitions of the divine nature to a formal administrative document known as an "Ekthesis." It lists the hierarchy of the Pentarchy—the five historic centers of Christian authority—and the independent (autocephalous) archbishoprics as they were recognized during the reign of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.</meta>

# + From the exposition made during the reign of the faithful emperor, Lord <note>original: kyrou</note> Alexios Komnenos +
# To the patriarchs of the imperial cities and the archbishoprics, 
# as well as to all other places in our lands.

First among the blessed patriarchs is the supreme high priest of Old <term>Rome</term>; by rank, he is the ecumenical pope of Old <term>Rome</term> and ecumenical patriarch.
Second is the one of <term>Constantinople</term>, <term>New Rome</term>; ecumenical patriarch.
Third is the one of <term>Alexandria</term>; archbishop of the great city of <term>Alexandria</term> and judge of the world; patriarch and pope of the great city of <term>Alexandria</term> <gloss>and in</gloss> all things a protector praying to God both for us, for our faith, and for our bodies, for the establishment and benefit of the fullness of Orthodox Christians everywhere.
Fourth is the one of the great [city] of God, <term>Antioch</term>, and of the East; holy patriarch and head of the hierarchy.
Fifth is the holy patriarch of <term>Jerusalem</term>, of all Syria, and of the holy city of <term>Jerusalem</term> and all Palestine and all that land; holy patriarch.

The independent <term>autocephalous: "self-headed," meaning a church that governs itself without being subject to a patriarch</term> archbishoprics are: 
1st: the archbishop of <term>Cyprus</term>.

# — An explanation of the ancient pyramids,
## recently, these had some sideways notations concerning them:

<margin>LL</margin>
It is worthy of wonder how the three "mountains" <note>original: "oron" — the author uses the word for mountains to describe the massive scale of the pyramids</note> of the aforementioned pyramids came to be there. It is known that if any other work were removed after such a long time, it would lose all its proportion and its venerable nature. For they say that the shape of the pyramids here was brought to light with complete reverence in its discovery, both because of their size and the variety of their construction. For these pyramids are among the buildings of the Egyptians. Built by the ancients to receive wheat <note>original: "pyrou" — grain or wheat. This reflects a common medieval and early modern belief that the pyramids were the "Granaries of Joseph" mentioned in the Bible</note>, of which the most were built in truth by the same impoverished kings who reigned, as Herodotus says <note>The author refers to the Greek historian Herodotus, though he misattributes the "poverty" of the kings; Herodotus actually emphasized their tyranny and the vast resources they spent</note>. For at the same time, he held the country. As for the pyramids, they are called so because of the shape of their construction; it comes from an imitation of fire <note>original: "pyros" — fire. Ancient authors often incorrectly thought the word "pyramid" was derived from the Greek word for fire, because the shape tapers upward like a flame</note>. For just as fire does, so do these taper from a wider base to a sharp point. They are square and four-sided, having equal sides and a single peak reaching toward the heights. These things, then, they say were explained to the orderly people, that is, perhaps, even on equal terms.

The notation is reflected sideways upon itself, as if reaching into the thousands, and sideways also, as one can see the entire Egyptian land is most fertile, though partitioned <note>original: "diapepodismene" — measured out or shackled, likely referring to the network of irrigation canals</note>. It is a wonderful and exceptional land. For the Nile clearly flowing past would not happen to be called a "goldsmith" <note>This may be a metaphorical reference to the wealth brought by the river</note>, but it is much used, and the most fertile part of the silt <note>original: "lypis" — likely a corruption of "ilys," meaning the fertile mud left by the river</note> of nature is promised. Where it also offers to all others, just as they say it lasts through the middle for many days or more. This refers to those things happening in the Delta on boats, and they recognize the seasonal changes <note>original: "pathe" — literally "passions" or "affections," here meaning the natural cycles or floods</note> of the great river. And there is the irrigation of the country, and the sun is great in the Delta. To release the spring at the source—and this we call the "horses" of the pyramids. Something of the fertility of the side, nor all the work of a woman <unclear>from them</unclear>

They say [these structures] are by a lake; and built for a multitude of loaves of bread <note>original: "arton" — bread. <margin>6. Concerning the lighthouse</margin>
And the **Lighthouse** <note>original: "Pharos" — the great lighthouse of Alexandria</note> situated in the harbor, being built; no longer admitting [others]; its utterance is acknowledged and the soul is its friend, but it is right for everything to have stood around it. As far as one may <unclear>sail</unclear>; a number; of the <unclear>island</unclear>. And of old, before all things, it has a length of seven stadia <note>original: "heptastadion" — the causeway that connected the island of Pharos to the city of Alexandria</note>. Those at sea did not grasp it; they show its side to be part of the harbor. Its nature and a great deal of the island's change of position; he who honored them more, being from God, made it; which that man, being holy, translated back from it. It stands off at such a great size that it serves instead of a tower. For it is likely that neither the one concerning whom they speak, nor the like, is held by it. And it is indeed so great, being carried in a circle from above; from where, burning long ago, they produce a flash of light. Another poetically [calls] these "passageways"; it stood in the sea as if the lighthouse were in the midst. <margin>7. Concerning the Colossus in Rhodes:</margin>
This **Colossus**, which is in **Rhodes**, partakes of the image of **Apollo**; standing from above like something suspended in the air. To all [structures] that lie before it, it immediately happened to have its size equal to them all together. For the sake of showing this, it was changed to an immense size. They say such was the architectural ingenuity that if one ever happened upon it from nearby in the sun, it could be seen from below and <unclear>...</unclear> having made such a physiognomy. Many things were well made, and a certain passage of such a pyramid, which is said to have required <unclear>excessive</unclear> camels for the purpose of carrying away such great things <note>A reference to the historical account that after the Colossus fell and lay in ruins, the bronze was eventually sold to a merchant who used hundreds of camels to transport the scrap metal</note>.

<margin>8. And of the Tomb of Mausolus:</margin>
This **Mausolus** was a tyrant of **Caria**, which is in **Phrygia** <note>The author incorrectly places Caria within the region of Phrygia; they were neighboring regions in Asia Minor</note>. In this desolate city, he prepared for himself a tomb, costly and most expensive. For it was said to keep away such things, because all the light of that <unclear>...</unclear> of that ancient sun, he heard of the thieves in the tombs. And this being for him a most ingenious construction, such as no other, which, being a burial of such size, shines forth among those things difficult to achieve. It is a glory to burn hope; it is quite wonderfully shaped into an image from the very whole. And he taught us that it is carried from **Cyzicus**; the [account] concerning that one in the place of the departed.

In this way, then, many indicate the struggle of those who came before. But the most wonderful portion of the cities in Assyria was the **walls of Semiramis** <note>A legendary queen of Babylon, often credited in antiquity with massive building projects.</note>, who rebuilt the foundations of her empire. Each side of them was forty-one stades <note>original: "stadion" — an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note> in length, and from this, the total perimeter happened to be the sum of those stades; the system of the city was four hundred and eighty stades. And there were lintels upon the walls, but the city occurred nowhere else like these; and in all its colors, it was beyond expectation, a sight unto itself.

The city’s title, named in the ancient accounts, did not originally come from Semiramis, but from the history of the ancient falls <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel</note> that befell them, so as to provide evidence that it was built according to the Tower and was a house of settlement—this is what the assembly of the **Theologian** <note>Likely Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, known as "The Theologian," who wrote on the "Confusion of Tongues."</note> calls it. <margin>Prayer before the Gospel</margin>
Illumine our hearts, O Master who loves mankind, with the pure light of Your divine knowledge. Open the eyes of our mind to the understanding of Your Gospel teachings. Plant in us also the fear of Your blessed commandments, so that, having trampled down all carnal desires, we may pursue a spiritual way of life, both thinking and doing all things that are well-pleasing to You. For You are the enlightenment of our souls and bodies, O Christ our God, and to You we give glory, together with Your eternal Father and Your all-holy, good, and life-giving Spirit, now and forever and to the ages of ages. Amen. 

And after the forgiveness <note>Referring to the mutual bow or rite of forgiveness between the clergy</note>, the priest, standing up, sends forth the deacon who is about to read the holy Gospel. The deacon, approaching the priest, makes a prostration and says in a low voice: "Bless, Master, the proclaimer of the holy Apostle and Evangelist <insert>Luke</insert>." And the priest says: "May God, through the intercessions of the holy and all-glorious Apostle and Evangelist <insert>Luke</insert>, give speech to you who proclaim the good news with great power, for the fulfillment of the Gospel of His beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ." 

And the deacon said: "Amen." And having venerated the holy Gospel, he takes it and goes out through the holy doors <note>The central doors of the icon screen or iconostasis</note> with lamps preceding him; and he stands upon the ambo <note>A raised platform or pulpit</note> or in the designated place. 

Then the deacon cries out: "Wisdom! Stand upright! Let us listen to the holy Gospel. Peace be to all." 
And the people: "And to your spirit." 
And the deacon: "The reading is from the holy Gospel according to <insert>Luke</insert>." 
The people: "Glory to You, O Lord, glory to You." 
The priest: "Let us be attentive." 

And after the Gospel is completed, the priest says: "Peace be to you who proclaim the good news." 
The deacon, returning as far as the holy doors, gives the holy Gospel back to the priest and begins the fervent litany <note>The 'Ektenis,' a series of intense petitions</note>. 

The deacon: "Let us all say with our whole soul and with our whole mind, let us say: O Lord Almighty, the God of our fathers, we pray to You, hear us and have mercy. brotherhood in Christ; and for all our fathers and brothers who have fallen asleep <note>A traditional Christian term for those who have died</note> before us.

<margin>The priest secretly</margin> O Lord our God, accept this fervent supplication from Your servants and have mercy on us according to the multitude of Your mercy, and send down Your compassions upon us and upon all Your people who await the rich mercy that comes from You.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological investigation into the nature of the human spirit. While the previous page utilized poetic "heroic meter" to describe the soul’s desire to return to God, this page shifts into a structured, catechetical (question-and-answer) format to define the tripartite division of the soul—a concept rooted in Platonic philosophy and adopted by Christian ascetic writers to explain moral struggle.</meta>

### Concerning the three parts of the soul: A Question:

**What is the virtue <note>original: "katorthoma" — literally a "straight action" or success; in a moral context, it refers to the perfect fulfillment of a duty or virtue.</note> of the rational part <note>term: <term>logistikon</term> (λογιστικόν) — the part of the soul responsible for reason, logic, and spiritual contemplation.</term> of the soul? Answer:**

The knowledge of divine exchanges <note>original: "hypallaktōn" — likely referring to the changing or alternating states of divine realities or the exchange between the human and divine.</note>; it is also naturally discerning of both the good and the evil. It signifies the practical order of the soul regarding the nature of the subject; it is an inscription of honor, as the essence [strives] toward the immutable and the best.

**Question: What is the evil and the failure <note>original: "ptaisma" — a stumble, slip, or moral error.</note> of the rational part? Answer:**

Impiety <note>original: "asebeia" — a lack of proper respect or "un-godliness" toward the divine.</note> concerning the divine; and primarily acting without knowledge or understanding, and being ignorant regarding what must be done; such as setting down laws for oneself and making these [errors] manifest.

**What is the evil movement of the desiring part <note>term: <term>epithymetikon</term> (ἐπιθυμητικόν) — the part of the soul associated with physical appetites, such as hunger, thirst, and sexual desire.</term>? Answer:**

To be occupied with the pleasure of desires and bodies, and every erotic power and passion, and to be nurtured around this appetite—unless one is a lover <note>original: "erastos"</note> of virtue and of the nature that fountains forth virtue.

**Question: What is the failure of the desiring part? Answer:**

Desire toward the things below; toward earthly and worldly bodies and weights; from which come love of possessions, love of glory, and greed <note>original: "philargyria" — literally "love of silver."</note>.

**Question: What is the virtue of the spirited part <note>term: <term>thymikon</term> (θυμικόν) — the "spirited" or "irascible" part of the soul, which governs anger, courage, and indignation.</term> of the soul? Answer:**

Hatred toward evil, and standing apart from the passions, and the soul’s readiness for virtue, and resisting sins even unto [the shedding of] blood.

**Question: What is the failure of such a part? Answer:**

Fear, hatred, lack of freedom <note>original: "aneleutheria" — a state of being unfree, often meaning stinginess or a servile disposition.</note>, lack of sympathy, love of strife, and pettiness <note>original: "mikrokakia" — literally "small-badness" or malice over trivial things.</note>.

Behold, then, the three parts of the soul and the end-point in corruption. And the rational part is located in the head; the spirited part in the heart; and the desiring part in the belly.

---

These things and the rest are immortal, directed toward the order of the political <note>note: "political" here refers to "politeia"—the way one conducts oneself as a member of a community or the "city of God."</note> salvation of the temperate and the things that follow from these.

...tactical experience and beauty; since it chooses to release [us] from the shifts of complex affairs and certain arranged words. But so much has been philosophized by such people, that though we have all fallen into these earthly things, the soul is not turned away from its sympathy for the blind. For it has been shown that the soul must be captured by a kind of divine capture <note>original: "halosis" — capture or conquest, often used in a mystical sense of being "seized" by God’s love or truth.</note>, and to live again among them, an idea has been recorded by them just as a certain beauty is for us. In addition to these, under <term>three hypostases</term> <note>The word "hypostasis" refers to a distinct person or individual reality—in this case, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who share one essence.</note> there is one nature, one deity, one energy, one grace, one power, and one will. -> **Distinguish the nature of things:** <-

Of things, some are **essentially good**; some are **essentially evil**; and some are **intermediate** <note>original: "mesa" — literally "middle things," known in Greek philosophy as "adiaphora" or things indifferent to salvation.</note>.

**Essentially good** are: **prudence, courage, temperance, justice**.
**Essentially evil** are: **folly, cowardice, licentiousness, injustice**.
**Intermediate** are: **wealth, poverty, glory, dishonor, health, sickness**; much lack of training follows these. 

All these intermediate things are called essentially neither good nor evil; rather, their nature depends on the **use** <note>original: "chresis"</note> we make of them, or the use made by those who possess them. For example: **wealth** is good if someone uses it with piety; but it is evil when it drives one toward empty pleasures and vanity. Likewise also **poverty**: it is good when it teaches us endurance, gratitude, and freedom; but it is evil when it gives birth to blasphemy and a lack of freedom because we cannot bear it. **Glory** is good when we use it for fellowship, or when it allows us to accept prudence and leads us to desire future glory; but it is evil when it hunts for praise from men and molds one into arrogance. Likewise also **sickness**: it is good when we use our patience for some action pleasing to God; but it is evil when it leads toward licentiousness and injustice in a similarly malicious way. For the world is painted in this way, and we use it: it is good [or] it is evil; for when it drives one to ingratitude, blasphemy, and grumbling, [it is evil]. **Great learning** is also good when we use it for teaching and the testing of true words; but it is evil when used for vainglory and the advocacy of injustice. **Beauty** is also good when it leads us to wonder at the well-being created by God and provides us with benefit; but it is evil when it persuades one toward fornicators and shameful things to learn, and does not know how to do what is proper. Likewise with the rest:

all things such as: **noble birth and low birth; beauty of form and ugliness; a beautiful voice and a harsh voice; strength and weakness; speed and slowness; skill and lack of skill**; and all such things. All these have their order and their value; and those who use them well are not ensnared by any of their harmful qualities. They should never be stripped away from them, but remain in their own place, unobserved and unadorned; and let persuasion harm the outward appearance, as if to move things for their own sake. None of the dispassionate things are given for evil, but they <note>The "they" likely refers to the passions or worldly desires.</note> want all desire and the lowly things to be honored, and for the best of our honor to be neglected. <meta>This page continues the manual of ecclesiastical discipline and liturgical practice. Having previously defined "essentially good" and "intermediate" things, the author now applies these principles to the specific rules of fasting, focusing on the transition from Cheese-fare week to Great Lent and the special status of Saturdays and Sundays.</meta>

# On the Holy and Great Sabbath

On the **Holy and Great Sabbath** itself <note>original: "Hagio kai Megalo Sabbato" — Holy Saturday, the day before Easter</note>, for two days, as if concerning a divine matter among us, the strictness of the fast was suspended from the glory of the holy ones. Our holy fathers, establishing their fasting diet, sought to contemplate everything divine regarding the Godhead and our worship. Therefore, we ask for the sequence of the fasts to begin from the avoidance of food. However, since the aforementioned path was not fully practiced during those days—specifically Wednesday and Friday of the **Cheese-fare fast** <note>original: "tyrines nesteias" — the week before Great Lent when dairy is permitted but meat is not</note>—we instead consume wine, cheese, and eggs, just as you would praise the **ancient pots** <note>original: "tas chytras" — likely a reference to the "Festival of the Pots" or specific vessels used for these lighter meals</note>.

The participation in these gifts is recognized as a matter of honor. Thus, the divine rule overlooks the "pot of the fast" for as much as is necessary. Clearly, it is forbidden to live on a full diet on that aforementioned day, as it precedes all the other days. Instead, they set forth the festival, which they freely associated with everyone. For throughout the entire **week of the Romans** <note>original: "hebdomada tes Romaion" — likely referring to Western/Latin practice or a specific calendar calculation</note>, we join in the honor of the Sabbath. We honor these days and guard them so that we may know the day of the fast healthily and piously, as determined by the rules concerning **Pascha** <note>original: "Pascha" — Easter</note> and the fast, just as was shown by the one who <unclear>delimited</unclear> the rules of Pascha.

It must be added that the beginning of the fast, starting from the Monday of **Cheese-fare** <note>original: "tyrophageos" — literally "cheese-eating"</note>, lasts through the entire week. This is not the same as every Saturday and Sunday. No longer should one offer divine gifts or cease all labors on these days as if they were a typical Saturday or Sunday. Rather, one should celebrate the Sabbath and the turn of the year; let there be a struggle. Let it not later be found that these things are mixed; it is good to be persuaded. Whether you wish to celebrate with the Saturdays and Sundays or without them, it concerns the week of Pascha. For the holy **Apostles** established this day from the outside, and all things are blessed in turn. For all the weeks and all the Sundays originate from their own Sabbath; and these are the celebrations of the week.

<column-break/>

They say that one should hold back until Sunday, under the very assembly of the day. And again, they should offer a blessing on the sixth day of the proclamation <note>original: "kerygmatos"</note>, toward that very day of the week. For its sake, the holy Apostles saw fit to fast the six days after the week of **Cheese-fare** <unclear>Cheese-fare</unclear> and the Saturday after that week. On that day and the six following days, one is expected to give back. Finally, it remains to fast on the Sabbath. By adding and introducing the commonality of the night of the Holy Sabbath to the six days, the honor has remained, by the grace of God, for all those who receive the Good News to fast until another nature—the dawning of the Sabbath, which is **Sunday** <note>original: "Kyriake" — the Lord's Day</note>.

One should also know this: if anyone does not follow the appropriate hour according to the **Greek custom** <note>original: "hellenikon ethos" — here meaning pagan or secular traditions of time-keeping</note>, they do not always act according to the opinion of the holy Apostles. A certain <term>Presbyter</term> <note>A priest</note> in the Peloponnese, named Peter, it was fitting that he should come to do reverence to me, the sinner, asking and entreating—having happened upon a debt—for a deliverance through the <term>habit</term> <note>original: "σχηματίσει" — refers to the "Schema," the formal dress and vows of a monk</note>. This blessed Peter, then, having appeared, and being eager to complete the lifestyle of those who lived in Palestine, having written down the training grounds and the gifts of his own life, withdrew by some means. He went quickly to his own fatherland, and he was moved to devotion in the place called "The Enclosure" <note>original: "ἐγκλείου"</note>. After a great deal of time, he fell into that region; after the rewards of his previous life, having received all the breath of his kinsmen, and with it he held his faith toward God.

<margin>+</margin> He placed them on a certain land, as inhabitants in mourning. When he saw me, he immediately stood praying, as I see my own affairs very quickly, by the power of his God and upon a certain hunger that was released from him. Regarding the spiritual work to <term>confess</term> <note>original: "ἐξορεῦσαι" / "ἐξαγορεῦσαι" — the practice of Exagoreusis, the vocal disclosure of thoughts to a spiritual father</note> my failings, for he wished to confess them to all in God-loving fellowship. **Taste** is perceptive of the qualities of flavor; and these are many. Within these senses, a certain **symmetry** <note>original: "συμμετρία" (symmetria) — a balanced proportion</note> is established by nature, so that they may naturally perceive the things they share in, and not just the symmetries themselves. Because of this, too much light destroys the sight, and a heavy sound destroys the hearing, and excessive fragrance or stench destroys the sense of smell. Likewise, an excess of bitterness carries away the taste, and extremes of heat and cold will dissolve the sense of touch.

For just as a king, surrounded by a bodyguard and never leaving his post, receives the experience of his territories through his attendants, in the same way, the **Mind** <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous) — the highest rational faculty of the human soul.</note> receives knowledge of sensory things through the senses, as if they were bodyguards. 

But while the mind is moved, the Divine is incorporeal and motionless, knowing all things even before they come into being, and needing no individual senses. It does not perceive through any intermediary among created things, but rather these senses are naturally caused by it. The Divine is outside of all complexity; it is simply one of the motions contemplated by the intellect. Or, if you speak of **motion** <term>motion</term> <note>original: "κίνησις" (kinēsis) — in ancient philosophy, this term refers to any kind of change, including growth, decay, and movement.</note> according to essence: for coming into being is the movement from nothing toward existence through **alteration** <note>original: "ἀλλοίωσις" (alloiōsis) — change in quality.</note>, while corruption is the movement from being toward non-being. The Divine is above all such motions of sensory things. For it is not moved by our impulses, nor toward any striving, for it is immortal and unchangeable. 

In every order, it is called "motion" when a created thing moves toward increase or decrease. "Alteration" is change according to some quality, or through the transition from one state to another; it proceeds and shifts from white to black, or from black to white. From the beginning, the Divine does not move with this kind of motion, nor does it move from weakness toward perfection; for it is without falsehood, entirely perfect, and the very source and cause of all good. How then could it be altered, or undergo any change?

A ransom <note>original: "λυτρῶμα" (lutroma)</note> is born by the one before it, and gives birth to the one after it. For those numbers of the encompassing circles of movement, the movements from which a **unity** <term>unity</term> <note>original: "μονὰς" (monas) — the number one, seen as the source of all numbers</note> is born, along with the unity with another; the fourth, and in four times four, and the four fours, and thirty-four; not five. And when these are composed with themselves, they give birth to a multitude. Likewise, those things born from one another also give birth together. For four times four is eight <note>The text here follows a symbolic rather than strictly mathematical logic common in late antique numerology</note> and a number, it gives birth to the eight times eight; but it does not give birth itself, because it exceeds the **decade** <note>the number ten, considered the number of perfection and completion</note>. But the number **seven** is not born by those before it; for through three or the whole, you have made six; and through two, it <unclear>pledges</unclear>. For when composed by itself, the decade... <note>The author is explaining why the number 7 is often called "the virgin" in Pythagorean and Christian numerology, as it is neither a product of factors within the decade nor does it produce another number within the decade when multiplied.</note>

Because of this, the **Father** is also called "Everything." And the Divine is also called "Father." There is no circumference to Him, and He is **Always Being**. He does not give birth to the multiplied and created nature from His own essence—those things being of a different birth—but rather they are sent forth from the Father, by whom they are moved and preserved. By the ancestors it was most wisely defined as a change of mixing, a shape of symmetry according to Him, looking toward us, the power of God. These things regarding the first names of the Father are poor and lowly, but regarding the offspring... how the beautiful relates to the failing, forgive me as a child, O **Shepherd of the gods** <note>A highly poetic and unusual title, likely referring to Christ as the leader of the saints or divine beings</note>; and toward this task which is beyond me...

<column-break/>

...they departed. Having proceeded:

-> + The words of the Lover of Mankind to his own soul: <-

Loosen the boundary of the ancient death; behold the profit of previous labors; long is the age <note>original: "αἰών" — refers to eternity or a vast span of time.</note> compared to the struggle of the soul's departure; in due time He will divide the soul from of old; He will cover the mind with a body upon the earth; the seed was choked among the thorns; no longer does desire give birth to anger; nor does the external world deem the empty mourning worthy; the scattering of longings is not visible; the weight of toils is a light gluttony; to dwell in rest upon a foundation; but not even from men here did He liken the body; you guarded the things even before the doors; I found no profit in the common things; what do they say, these things in which I delight under the mind? But the things before me have been paid in full; everything was flowing away and could not bear to see anything; beloved nowhere; what is the character? To attain the toils of the ancient proverbs; let it depart before I know possession again; how shall I not run again with grief in my soul? How not toward tension? How by the springs? How shall I cast off the snare of the evil one, which has girded you all, who are disjointed; and the end of the much-hymned wings; into the complete cessation of sins; but as a branch of God having once disciplined; by my cleansing of the filth of vanities; I will pity my soul, as if newly born before the beginnings of my dwelling place.

# + On the Sun, set apart from the Chaldean instruments: the Chaldean Oracles:
## + Whether it is more specific, and the whole is "shining on both sides": An Inquiry: 1

<margin>1</margin>
If it is said among the philosophers that the innate parts of the cosmos happen to be smaller than those others; for instance, the things in this world; and in their form, they are irrational, and these irrational things exist according to the powers of the <term>irrational soul<note>original: "ἀλόγου ψυχῆς" — in Neoplatonic thought, the part of the soul responsible for basic life functions and emotions, distinct from the rational mind.</note></term> within it; and the powers in the body and its parts. And there, the divine aspects of such powers; let it have its own specific irrational parts and its irrational powers; or [act] irrationally. And the irrational parts are nature; and of nature, the body; and that which is under the mass of <term>matter<note>original: "ὕλης" (hyle) — the raw physical substance of the universe, often seen as a "precipice" or a trap for the soul.</note></term>. Regarding this Chaldean theory, he says that if one wishes for "irrationality" <note>original: "ἀλογίαν" — literally a lack of reason or speech.</note> while having no rational connection within it; and thinking that [other] thing to be worse, he says: that it is more specific; that which is <term>shining on both sides<note>original: "ἀμφιφαής" (amphiphaes) — a term often applied to the Moon, which receives light from the Sun on one side and faces the Earth on the other; here used metaphorically for the soul's state.</note></term> upon the whole. For he would say this first: either the irrational soul possesses [this light] for all, having been purified from the "fiery" state, he says, into the region above the moon, after the dissolution of our body and the things that fulfill the "shining on both sides" of the whole; that is, appearing from both sides, and having its existence illuminated at once by the "shining on both sides." From above, darkness is perceived from both sides toward the gods, in the light, or the things written there. And where is this, and correctly so, both itself and that which gives light; and also toward the lunar part. For he says it is such: for it illuminates this toward the lower parts; and in this way, there is a mystical illumination; nor is the whole "shining on both sides" beneath the moon. It becomes entirely illuminated. One must therefore state the Oracle: for the heaven is full of souls purified from the earth beneath the moon, the "shining on all sides," but a portion of its zodiac signs, or the whole earth happens [to be so]. For the "shining on both sides" will be allotted to the whole when the entire soul is cast out pure from the body, whence the purified soul is placed by the sun as immortal according to the irrational soul; it leads back those who happen to be beneath the moon. And the Chaldean Oracle says, purifying it and agreeing with the Oracle:

<column-break/>

### How the Material World was Born, and Why it is Untiring

The **Hecatine Strophalos** <term>Strophalos<note>original: "στρόφαλος" — literally a "spinning thing." For upon these things, the work often [shows] the more divine characteristic. This would shine forth in the body and be prepared through nature. For even the passions, along with matter, are in the bodies; for from the same things comes the passion, which therefore is not useful or strong. But the ensouled living body is not filled [by light]; yet concerning the edge, as if in matter, and having grown weary of this beauty, he filled it with light. When the soul has separated, the poor [element] will arrive, and it shall walk about being "limb-loosing" <note>original: "λυσιμελοῦσαν" — a poetic epithet for sleep or death, here likely meaning the relaxation of the body's grip on the soul</note>. For every completion of glory from the new to those who are strong... not before it itself [received] the virtues from him; having supplied the whole cause... the Father of Instruction <note>original: "ὁ τῆς παιδεύσεως πατήρ"</note>, no longer this whole house, a completer of goods for us and our parents; an abundance of humble things. Which is called the "first"; fulfill the power of the matter, having the strength; as he himself, where things are worse, he is of the Great Father, the cause of all demiurgy <term>Demiurgy<note>original: "δημιουργίας" — the act of crafting or creating the physical universe</note></term>. For together, alongside subtle spiritual breaths <note>original: "πνευματικά"</note>, he brought it forward entirely; the characteristic of the provision of created things; he gave them toward the first-most of becoming. For indeed, every [thing] is infinite; for some he allows to be in agreement, for others formless.

<column-break/>

...of the light toward itself, being drawn in from faith; so that everything, whatever it may be, bellows, even of the dissolving natures, and just as I said of any chance thing, in the likeness of those which exist well in the material passions. And not only to those full of passions which torment them, but also to those [moving] into the immaterial <note>original: "ἀΰλου" — without matter</note> state, well-ordered by symmetry. For even through evil, through the sense-perceptible matter and the arrival into birth, it is not so much spiritual as it is... for many things being united, and the bodies becoming despondent, so that it seems a world of misfortunes is brought together upon the city. Since, having taken pleasure even in this, and I saw it, having descended to all its own, not in any way will it shine forth, the first [light] which happens even beyond sense-perception. These things are placed even in fortunes, painfully upon it; and the things from his poor system, not so simply, but even the things lying above every order are diminished. And one thing is that which generates; but the spiritual existences of the bodies—and it is both incorporeal and psychic—but by the agreements with the worlds. These things which are brought together are the virtues, and the thing caused by them is virtue—lying above. A source of spiritual things in the soul, most pure; he sees not naked, nor hearing the smoke of it, he will no longer speak. Therefore the natural soul, leaving the body in labors, I will guard this same thing as a stranger; they adorn virtue for the faithful; and grace holds the vessels for them; to the noble ones, and the spirit will draw into the body. They shall leave life, and it may happen that it must be said, with the presiding lady, everything has ceased. For the soul, being fire <note>original: "ψυχὴ πῦρ οὖσα"</note>, they shine like fire, a movement of immortality, just as someone said... and yet many things are the Fullness <term>Pleroma<note>original: "πλήρωμα" — the "fullness" or totality of divine powers</note></term> and fire; the soul being immaterial and incorporeal fire, organizing the cooperation of matter and of the material darkness, even if it is in them; nor can its own things remain likenesses.

The discourse is about the passions; that with the underlying things, he distinguishes the generation.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the soul's journey by situating it within a vast, hierarchical cosmos. While the previous page dealt with the soul's release from Fate and bodily passions, this section describes the divine "architecture" through which the soul descends and must eventually re-ascend, specifically focusing on the "Chaldean Oracles"—a set of mystical texts from the 2nd century AD that blended Platonic philosophy with ritual practice.</meta>

...systematic, or even wonderful voices; joining the revel; delightful both in dignity and simplicity, providing pleasure in both their utterance and their naming. From where do they flow? A vocalized and guiding Will. This is how it came to be: These <term>Iynges</term> <note>original: "ἴϋγγες" — in the Chaldean system, these are divine "wheels" or mediators that transmit the Father's will and the thoughts of the Mind to the lower worlds</note> are Ideas, the mother of the <term>Noetic Depth</term> <note>original: "νοητοῦ βυθοῦ" — the "Intelligible Abyss," the profound, unknowable essence of the supreme Divine</note>, encompassed by three sources. For just as the Father encompasses all, so too does He contain them within Himself beforehand. And the "Counsels of the Father," because of their intellectual excellence, are carried forth ineffably, standing ready and awakened by their own generative existence—ineffably. For they are the tokens of the mysteries being set apart, intellectually; and being generatively brought forth by the Second Mind, they are carried as if ignited, following the intellectual movements before the processions. Just as these things give birth to the Father, though they do not know the intellectual ranks—even if they give birth to the very same things—so too do the intellectual activities become the pretexts or foundations, being ineffable in their existence for the one who declared they should be. This is an exposition of the main points from the body of the <term>ancestral doctrines</term> <note>original: "πατροπαραδότων δογμάτων" — teachings handed down from the "fathers" or ancient sages</note>.

Over all are three magical worlds: first, the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>original: "ἐμπυρίῳ" — the highest, "fiery" realm of pure intellect</note>; and three <term>Aetherial</term> worlds after it; and finally, three <term>Hylic</term> <note>original: "ὑλικοῖς" — material or physical</note> worlds. The last of these is called the "Chthonic" or Earthly world, and there is a single light-giver which is the sublunary realm—this possesses that matter which they call the Abyss. They glorify one Principle of all things, and they declare the whole world to be under it. Next, he speaks of a certain "Fatherly Dyad," which is blended from three <term>Triads</term>. Each Triad possesses Power and Mind, which has created all things. After these, there are Channels: the <term>Empyrean</term>, the <term>Aetherial</term>, and the <term>Hylic</term>. And those within the elements are the <term>Teletarchs</term> <note>original: "τελετάρχαι" — "masters of the rites" or cosmic initiators who oversee the boundaries of the different worlds</note>. After these are the Source-Fathers, who are also called <term>Cosmagoi</term> <note>original: "κοσμαγοί" — "world-guiders" or planetary rulers</note>. Of these, the first is the "Once Beyond," who is supplicated as the <term>Monad</term> <note>original: "μονάς" — the "One" or the indivisible source</note>. From there, "Beyond," things are turned three ways toward the gods; and there are "above-life" ends, worshiping the Father and the source of all triads, and Truth, and Love. And they say...

<column-break/>

...is also the beginning of the lot, from the Solar <term>Father</term>; and the beginning of rites; and the source of sense-perception; and the source-like Faith; and the source of lightning-bolts; and the first Source; and the Characterizing source. They preside over the known sources, being released from the source-realms again; such as Iris and Hermes. And they call these the "Drawn Sources": the center and the element, and the "Girdle." And they call the "Beginning of Metals" a source. They make the "Faiths" to be principles, which are the cause and contemplation for the principles above them. Of the "Life-generating" principles, the summit is called a "Source" in that place; the middle is the "Source of Principles"; and the end is "Governing." They place there a "Fatherly Mind" and a "Vital Cause," as if in three solar-lit worlds. And the world is girdled; as a vital power, they place the *Parapis*, the *Strapis*, and Nature. And this is the Sphere of Wisdom and the Source-like Oracle. Speaking as intellectuals, they say that the Earth is carried straight and is girdled, and that fire is established in the middle of the ages. It gives life to the celestial zones, which are released and go around, and to those who inhabit the five zones. For he says there are gods over all the heavens, whose "lines" partition the creations of the world. There is also a vital portion of the solar fire which is encompassed. After the zones is the "Fixed Circle," encompassing the seven spheres upon which the stars reside. He says there are other "Spiritual Worlds" serving the Aetherial Depth, and others "Life-zoned" in which the Seven reside. Of the "Fixed Fates," which are all sources, they attribute to them the power of foreknowledge and the "Source-Soul." This Soul proceeds from the Empyrean according to the Will of the <term>Father</term>. She also possesses a generative status and is "Self-Living." For he says: "Another is the sound." There is also a source-like portion of the fire, the residence of the Divine and the "Sword-Fire." I saw the Father-like, standing immaterial and <term>self-subsisting</term> <note>original: "αὐθυπόστατον" — existing by itself, not dependent on anything else for its being</note>. This is the divine spark from Him. They say there is a Fortune, and even a "Source-Fortune." Along every path, the lightning of the Source and the terrifying Will are shown forth...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on the soul's journey, transitioning from the celestial "architecture" of the previous page to the specific teachings of the great masters—Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus—regarding the soul's relationship with the physical world and the path to purification through dialectic and dispassion.</meta>

the soul, again within the world, even if some [souls] are drawn back into it, or even into the earth itself. They held that the world is eternal, as is the period of the stars. They describe Justice <note>original: "δίκην" — here likely referring to the cosmic order or the goddess Dike</note> as a sea, and within this world, they name her a goddess, speaking of a "terrestrial dance" <note>This refers to the rhythmic, choreographed motion of the elements and living things on Earth, mirroring the celestial dance of the stars</note>. He also speaks of the irrational soul <note>original: "ἄλογον ψυχὴν" — the part of the soul responsible for instincts and bodily functions, which lacks reason</note>, and for it too hastens toward the "remaining part" or the "vessel," but in some cases, it might have a sympathetic connection <note>original: "συμπαθῶς" — refers to "cosmic sympathy," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected</note> toward it, and the influence of a particular reason might strike it. Regarding the cosmic arrangement toward stillness for all things, from the highest folds to the middle, and from the terrestrial materials, they say that **the things above have sympathy for the things below** <note>A fundamental Neoplatonic principle: the celestial realms influence the earthly realm through a natural resonance</note>, and especially for the realm beneath the moon. It restores the souls—those in what is called "death"—according to the Stratonicean <note>original: "στρατωνικὰς" — possibly a reference to a specific school of thought or a lost ritual tradition</note> ways and purifications. This happens either entirely in that part of the world, or for all, even those acting above the world. And they define these souls as monads <note>original: "μονὰς" — units of being that are indivisible</note>, consisting of both indivisible and divisible natures. This, then, is the sum of the doctrines; the majority and the best of these were perfected by those around the "Amelichian" <note>original: "ἀμελιχον" — likely a scribal error for Amelius, a student of Plotinus</note> school of Plotinian writing. And the divine voices <note>original: "θεῖαι φωναὶ" — a standard way to refer to the "Chaldean Oracles"</note> are in communion with these matters, and they were set forth from the power of Plotinus.

For it is a disease <note>original: "Νόσημα" — referring to the "sickness" of the soul when it is trapped in material concerns</note>, even when occurring according to nature, and the thoughts of life are guided by art and reason—how they approached a certain state, as they say. Instead of that "mode," those things are not struck, nor would anyone say they have heard of the nature of pleasure, nor the "breeze" and the things from there, for those who participate in the "interweaving" <note>original: "συμπλοκῆς" — the entanglement of the soul with the body</note>, whether well or otherwise, they come to be. And where there is interweaving, there is perception <note>original: "αὔθησις" for "αἴσθησις"</note>; but perception occurs after the judgment of thoughts, or the doubt in knowledge, for in this way these things also exist.

<column-break/>

And if again it is otherwise, possessing the imagination <note>original: "φαντασίαν"</note>, or if delusion <note>original: "τύφον" — literally "smoke" or "vapor," used to describe the mental fog of vanity and false pride</note> arises within; for some of those who are accurate in these things also experience forgetfulness. For accuracy is a falling away from the things of life... and the "now" is no better than any other example of discernment. This discernment is twelvefold... and these things remained the same as those of **Dialectic** <note>original: "διαλεκτικῆς" — for Neoplatonists, this was the highest science, the process of rising from particulars to the contemplation of True Being</note>. He learned or was educated in the forms of these things: pro-passion, freedom from passion <term>apatheia</term>, and the state of passion <term>empatheia</term> <note>These terms describe the soul's emotional state: "pro-passion" is the initial impulse, "apatheia" is the goal of the sage (freedom from irrational emotion), and "empatheia" is being subject to those emotions</note>. For the bitterness of bodily things is a "state of passion"; but the soul's own relation toward these passions is what it is. He accuses those in the [undivided?] state of "delusion," since the ancients gave many such things, both good and bad, whether passionate or impassive—except that he does not mean "passion" in the sense of a movement toward suffering. He will rest the "blessed state" in both ways: "passion" because of the neglect of the city's sobriety, and for those who do not neglect it. But "freedom from passion" <note>original: "ἀπάθεια"</note> exists because of the activity of the un-neglecting parts, having a counter-balancing reasoning <note>original: "λογισμοῦ"</note>. And again, among the passions, it is not a matter of "freedom" in another sense, but holding "freedom from passion" as a middle point. For **freedom from passion is the stillness of the various burdens** <note>original: "ὄγκων" — "bulks" or "masses," referring to the heavy, material concerns that weigh down the soul</note>. The things from the soul are "passionate" because of the earth and what is near it; but if someone is [purified] because of the holy and this delight, it is a "passion" through the holy and the near. But these things are "impassive" for him if they are... [text ends abruptly].

<summary>This page discusses the cosmic "sympathy" between the celestial and terrestrial realms, citing the authority of Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus. It also explores the psychological states of the soul, specifically focusing on "dialectic" and the achievement of "apatheia" (dispassion) as a means of quieting the "burdens" of material existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the pseudo-Aristotelian "Problems," a genre of literature that explores natural phenomena through a question-and-answer format. Horses and the rest of the animals <unclear>do not grow increasingly</unclear> <unclear>bald</unclear>, yet it happens to them, and they also experience graying in old age, just as humans do. Almost all other creatures preserve the same color. Gray hairs are white because the cause of old age is a certain <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: phlegma; in ancient medicine, this was one of the four humors, considered cold and moist</note>, or perhaps a lack of <term>concoction</term> <note>original: pepsis; the process of "cooking" or maturing bodily fluids through internal heat</note>. In those things that possess color, such as bones, whiteness is not mixed in like phlegm. Why is it that in old age we first produce gray hairs on the head, but not on the eyelashes? It is because the first hair is scorched by a certain bitterness. Moreover, because it is at the extremity of the body, it tends to pour out the <term>phlegms</term> of the majority. This is shown by the preservation of these same things in the nostrils. All those who are afraid are cold, because the breath is preserved by the mouth. Also, because of fear, the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: pneuma; the vital breath or gaseous substance thought to carry life and sensation</note> suffers a certain motion. Just as after fears, the <term>residues</term> <note>original: perittomata; waste products of digestion or metabolism</note> themselves contribute toward the safety of the body's life. Fear releases the blood along with itself, just as it does the lungs. This occurs because the body defines itself through heat. For everything that moves, the body is warm; one might philosophize that the thing producing motion and rest is the <term>spirit</term>. Being swift and turning, it is from this that heat is perfected. Why is it that both those in sorrow and those laughing weep? Those in sorrow do so because the spirit of the ocular pores squeezes out the moisture within them. For sorrow, through cooling and thickening, draws out what is in the pores. But those who rejoice pour out the moisture from the pores; however, this does not happen for the delight of the eyes, but rather from the hearts being moved. 

Why do those who see someone yawning, yawn themselves? It is because the sight prepares a similar memory. This happens even more among irrational animals. For it is not that the sight is deceived, but that others suffer the same thing in sympathy. Why do those with <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>an ancient term for inflammatory eye diseases</note>, if they see another with the same condition, suffer it themselves? They sympathize with the sufferer. It is not that they suffer from bitterness, but why through the eyes from the evil? It even feels well. Since the <term>spirit</term> pours forth from the eye, it is not contained. In sight, it is just as in the sense of smell. For the affections of the spirit are easily changed by the air in the blood, and the matters of sight are laid around it. Therefore, sight also, because of the essence in each discharge, <gloss>adds</gloss> health to the essence there.

Is it added from the sight? Regarding things that are far off by the spirit, we see the strike immediately, but we hear the sound later. And even before the blood, do we see the strike of the <unclear>under-standing</unclear>? It is because the sense of hearing is carried down like a spirit in a river, and it receives the breath from the air; it is necessary for the whole air to be divided to bring the strike to the ear as if in a river. See then what it receives: both the strike of the hearing of the spirits, and by the strike of the spirit, the sight which is seen before it. So that even when we see the hearing, and upon the strike of the spirits, the results of sight are perfected.

Why do they not see things lying close at hand, but see those far away accurately? In the soul, it is because of a vehemence toward the things in that part, because it does not travel toward the hour of anything <note>this may refer to the "eye-beams" or visual rays believed to exit the eye in ancient optics</note>, due to its particularity. <unclear>Many</unclear> things appear all at once to the sight toward the honey. The light shifts toward the affection of the person. Why, among the thick-haired plants, are there those like the olives? Or those with thick hair? It is because the majority of hairs are contained by the spirit, and it makes the hair grow. This is true for all, stemming from dry substances. But the cause is found in the motion. The spirit being in excess, and especially because it is strongly attractive, they perfect it through the moisture of the spirit. Why are some things revealed by the sun from those that are to be, while others are not? Because some things are variegated and change similarly by chance, and especially like a flame, the spirit is similarly entwined, so that it <unclear>is</unclear> through the fire itself. And some things pertain to colors and thinning. The cold also moves, even before the rush of the crystals through them. Why does whiteness occur in old age, and the skin and such things become white? But not for all to a lesser degree. ...then it does not act; for since heat is a cause of scorching and destruction, fire is released while the heat surrounds the air. **Why** is warm water in wells more drinkable? Or should we compare it to sweet things? It is because wells possess a "long flavor" <note>likely referring to a lingering or deep-seated quality</note>, which comes from the warm water. Most wells have no outflow <note>original: ekphrasin; a way for the water to escape or circulate</note>, which is why the water drips out. For others, the cold is actually the cause of the warm water <note>a reference to the ancient theory of antiperistasis, where opposites intensify each other by compression—e.g., external cold trapping heat underground</note>. **Why** do infants stop crying when they are lying prone <note>face down</note>? Is it because they press their bellies outward? This involves the proportions of bodies and the <term>breaths</term> <note>original: pneumata; the vital gases or spirits that move through the body</note>. For if they were to turn over, perhaps the pressure makes the voices cease.

**Why** is it that by blowing, we can either cool things down or warm up cold things? It is because the <term>breath</term> <note>original: anapnoē</note> is inherently warm, as is the spirit of life. The movement itself produces heat, while the cold object is that which is being warmed. Why then the movement? Is it due to the "pouring together"? Or is it because the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: pneuma</note> is thick and powerful? For excellence is a kind of coldness, becoming thick because of the cold and the nature of the sun. It is not by the same cause that the air acts and becomes warm; rather, it is a thickening of the cold. Persistence is a "thick" thing. Where it is not possible for the heat to surround and burn, the opposite occurs. Or is it that they do not see in the middle of the day, but they do see at night? This is because they have a very subtle <term>visual spirit</term> <note>original: optikon pneuma; the substance ancient Greeks believed shot out of the eye to "touch" objects and enable sight</note>. When it is moderately thickened, it is prepared for seeing; but in the tension and the bright light, the delicate spirit, once thickened, is dispersed and scattered.

**Why** do many people fail to see things that are far away and black, yet they can see things that are far away and white? Just as in the middle of everything, white things remain visible. It is because the visual spirit, being extremely subtle and reaching far, becomes dispersed and lightened. The hair... <unclear>visible things</unclear>... especially to see the first things. The fine-grained and pure things. But some people can see things that are far away...

<column-break/>

...and it pours forth when prone. But it does not do this for those who are prone because their visual spirit is thick. For they lack the ability to move and be breathed upon; therefore, it always tends toward the ground. Or is it because of the "wandering" of the vision?

<margin>+</margin>
**Why** is salt dark when it is first gathered, but natron <note>original: litra; a naturally occurring soda ash used for cleaning</note> is whiter? Is it because the salt is heaped up in a dense mass? This is because of the material being acted upon toward the white. The <unclear>salt-workers</unclear> near us are turned dark by the scorching of the heat. But natron, being purified by something else or by other means, and not being scorched by the sun, has a nature that burns again to serve. Again, the old and original salt is whiter in its state than what was once dark. But the old whiteness is not the same; it is hard and thick. If they broaden it and make it thick and <unclear>voiceless</unclear>.

**Because** again, the breadth of them, and the cheese, and the things lying there, just as this wine is similar to them, are they not typical?

<margin>+</margin>
**Why** is it that when people are excessively angry, their eyes become fiery? This is why they call anger a "boiling around the heart" <note>original: kardias zesin; the standard Aristotelian definition of the physical aspect of anger</note>, and they link anger to fire. This explains the "how." In agony, because the eyes seem to disappear, a turning-back is visible, and this is the cause. Hence the face appears red. Because of the anxieties, we see water being preserved, and this happens quickly.

**Because**... of the fields, they act separately, which is why these things were called "fire." This contributes to the loss of thickness, as the heat takes it away by the attack of the warmth. And those who are long... <unclear>preserving him with tremors</unclear>. And the spirit happens to be full, not by chance... just as the malicious person and the one who prevails more often happen to enjoy themselves. This contributes to the movement received by the bodies.

<margin>+</margin>
**Why**... determined by chance? Because for those who sail, one must do what is beneficial. And by striking and irritating the bodies, one part is moved toward the bodies of another. This is where they suffer most. How are the things with the <unclear>sister</unclear> toward the bodies...

**Why** is it that some who are drunk—or indeed all—see double? Is it because they fill the area in front of the eyes with a mass <note>likely referring to a "filling" of humors or vapors</note> and the eyes become relaxed, so that this eye flees further away for everyone, and the same images do not coincide? Rather, the rays of the eyes do not converge on the same part of the visible object, but on different parts. Thus, what each eye sees remains distinct, which is why a single object appears as a multitude.

**Why** does the hare sleep with its eyes closed <note>original: συγκαμμύει (synkammuiei); however, ancient tradition usually claimed hares slept with eyes open—the text here may be debating the physical structure of the eyelids</note>?
<margin>a</margin> Because it is delicate and has a squinting nature; its parts, such as the male organs, are naturally fused to the ridges <note>likely referring to the eyelids or anatomical structures around the eye</note>, making it impossible for them to close fully. Since nothing is covered over them, sight enters more quickly.

**Why** does the "white water" <note>possibly referring to a specific type of discharge or thin fluid</note> of colts freeze in the cold, yet fire does not enter it? Because oil is vaporous and more well-tempered, whereas that which is most cold and vigorous is not caused by <term>breath</term> <note>original: pneuma; vital air or spirit</note> or frost in the cooling. Water is vaporous; it is not a thin liquid. Therefore, it alone freezes, for that which is just before the source is small and the passage is not superior.

**Why** do birds become parched and delicate? For this reason, regarding the swan itself, they say nothing is ever constant in their speech, but for others, they say that excessive urination occurs. The dryness toward the upper parts takes up the lower parts as well. This is also why children are deaf—not all, but some—because from a well-flowing source everything is similar, but from others, not all are deaf. For this bitter moisture is the cause of all falling away of this desire <note>likely a reference to the loss of a faculty</note>.

**Why** do the upper parts of the head grow hair, while the parts below the head do not grow it in the same way? Because, just as with all high and lofty things, hair does not grow from the same place. The lower parts are the points where the upper hairs sprout. These completed parts are the lower ones, and their colors are among the most fortunate; for their natures are well-disposed.

**Why** do some wheats grow only when held and in excess, while others grow during the time of weaving? Because nature has known the creation of such things, everything that comes from the liver, which is why it surpasses the majority.

<column-break/>

On the chance of those things which grow out and adorn, they take their origin.

**Why** are the eyes of those who have been "burned" <note>likely referring to fever or intense internal heat</note> hollow? Because of a strong consumption of the <term>breath</term> <note>original: pneuma</note> of the body, which either stores up the art itself or moves those things already bounded. For where something laughable can arise from a metaphor, a man becomes boastful because of the abundance of the streams. The smaller things—those which were said to be formed in them—how is this? Because of the multitude of things being formed, it jumps away from the majority, like a pig. And the birds and fish: as many as are lamps, all are like some sieve of change, as is the custom for those who have drunk. For the things that come before birth and the sources are like those of wolves, and those made bitter from them. For as many as are in the ebb-tide, they are the protection of the octopuses, for these things are in everything.

**Why** is the milk of goats bitter when they are nursing? It brings destruction upon them. Because they bear young before old age. This is because of the bitterness of all of them; hence some do not even consider them living beings, and they place the remains of their digestion there.

**Why** are the most prominent things not...? Because the first things and bodies are as many as occur by chance.

**Why** does a living creature shiver and its hair stand on end? Because these sufferings occur due to certain frequent breaths <note>original: pnoiais</note> of the pores of the skin gathering together. For it surrounds everything; why then do they stand upright?

**Why** is it helpful to apply dressings diagonally on wounds because of these conditions? Because it is exceedingly moist and dry; for it makes the waves toward it, and the peculiar impulse and motion caused by the conditions.

**Why** did hair grow on the forehead of the body? Nature produced covers for these parts in such a way, through which everything around the body is quickly distinguished. For not through everything does it produce all evil with them; it does not place the hair there to start the knowledge of the breaths, but has given the use of each of the limbs for ease and beauty, to restrain the passions.

**Why** is the dark-skinned person entirely... and never...
