<margin>120</margin> ...if he catches no beast <note>original: θῆρα (thēra) — refers to any wild animal or prey</note> at all, he will encounter difficult entanglements and error. He will also face dangers in the ranks of battle from his own parents, his relatives, and his friends. He will suffer, and simply put, he will live with fear and experience grief.

---

<margin>121</margin> ...of temptation; from innate causes: If hares <note>original: λαγοί (lagoi)</note>, whether in the fields, appear without fur <note>original: γυμνοφοροῖεν (gymnophoreien) — possibly meaning "bare-skinned" or "exposed"</note>, wandering and being beautiful, the dreamer will find himself drawn toward grace and will find a wife of such a character. If he cuts them or prepares them as food, he will gain wealth from them. If he sees himself eating the whole flesh of a hare, he has received wealth with joy, but also a disease from it; according to his travels, he will suffer such a thing and be overtaken by it. If one sees a hunting party with a certain <unclear>noise</unclear>, he will prosper with a great amount of wealth and achieve what he desires. However, he will encounter fears, bile, and bitterness from these things—as in ancient times and now—resulting from the humors <note>original: ὑγρῶν (hygrōn) — refers to the four bodily humors of Hippocratic medicine</note> and from drinking.

---

<margin>122</margin> Mice <note>original: μύες (myes)</note> represent a wicked enemy; one should guard his own house against them. If they come without honor, he will fight them with words. If someone sees muzzles <note>original: κημωνὶ (kēmōni) — likely a trap or restraint</note> or snares, it signifies the distress and stumbling of a wicked enemy. If he sees his clothes being eaten by them, it signifies the exhaustion of wealth and the diminishing of his glory. If dogs appear, it signifies that such an enemy will come to his full potential. If he sees tangled or muddy dogs, he will find the wealth of a dishonorable person. If someone sees <note>original: πικουσοίται (pikousoitai) — an obscure term, perhaps a corruption of a word for "stinging" or "biting"</note>, he will find fear and sickness, and deceit from a stranger. Dogs from the flocks represent joy, since the enemy is a foreigner. If he strokes them, it is a matter of luck. If kings see themselves drinking among their leaders, it signifies deceits or temptation, or falling in war against those who have revolted—both kin and those within the city walls. In general, the kingdom prepares for all outcomes. For leaders, the dream is judged according to the time and the circumstances.

---

<margin>123</margin> Generally, when one judges a woman with a wicked face, he will encounter death in a war of faith; she is a thief and is insatiable. She is your light, yet she is also a deceit, coming from useless things—a stranger

<column-break/>

dragging you along. If one sees someone hanging, it concerns the wealth of another <unclear>...</unclear>. But if they are wicked—for he who drinks their juices <note>original: κρεάδων (kreadōn) — meat-juices or broth</note>—it benefits his health and everything else. If he sees that every kind of wicked creature is at war with him, he will find a disease that brings him down. If the wild boar <note>original: κάπρος (kapros)</note> defeats him, he will suffer a long illness and be greatly wronged. Regarding the pig: from innate causes, it will appear to all. Pigs represent a fallen enemy. If one sees himself fighting a pig, it signifies a powerful and well-equipped warrior; this status is seen through authority alone. Otherwise, if he sees what was said regarding the dog, it is judged as a wicked thing. If a poor man <note>original: πτωχὸς (ptōchos)</note> drinks from it, he will find distress and punishment; the unexpected "poor man's drink" will enslave a manic enemy. If a poor man sees this, his wealth will vanish immediately. If the king gathers a drink and he himself flows with the dogs, it means an enemy who is hard to repay in words; it remains and shines forth. If there is a multitude of the pig species and he departs to the judges, he will be diminished, though only moderately. If he sees himself eating pork, he will find gold, and wealth will be established through it. If he sees himself walking among pigs, he will find swift joy. If someone sees horns on an enemy, they belong to that enemy; he has evaded the horns. If a king sees such a thing of a young pig, he will have wonderful goods and will have conquered the enemy. If he sees donkeys or authorities from the poverty of those pigs, he will find an enemy who has been circumvented <note>original: πεπλοίου (peploiou) — possibly "sailed around" or "outmaneuvered"</note>, whom wealth follows. If he sees the armor of leaders or the heads of a pig, the meaning is the same: he will gain the "head" <note>original: κεφάλαιον (kephalaion) — a pun meaning both the physical head and the financial capital</note> of his enemy's wealth. These things happen to all, concerning the poor and enemies alike, from innate causes.

<margin>Section 180</margin> **Concerning dragons and snakes; from the small serpents and those that belong to them:**
A dragon <note>original: δράκων (drakōn) — in ancient dream interpretation, a 'dragon' was typically a massive serpent, symbolizing a king, a high official, or a powerful spiritual force</note>, or however one might <unclear>say</unclear> to some regarding horses and snakes: since these represent wicked and minor enemies, judge them as messengers of [the enemy's] methods. If one sees a wicked dragon appearing there, bringing a <unclear>staff</unclear> to a father, it shows that an enemy is among them to be dealt with. If the dragon should fall from a <unclear>heat</unclear> and be uprooted, the dreamer will find that a person of honor will be moved and uprooted. If he sees a dragon and is afraid of its passing, he will fight against a king or an unstable enemy who is being registered [against him]. If it brings wealth, it also brings loss. If he sees whatever kind of dragon appears to him, he will find fear coming from the king. But if he sees it as a corpse speaking to him fearlessly, he will <unclear>follow</unclear> after wealth. The dragon having arrived: if he sees a dragon and hears a wicked obedience, he will find wealth and another will attend to the king. If he sees the nature of a dragon, either in its size or in a desert place, it represents a mighty king or an old enemy. If there are many of them, they represent the royal court; this is suitable for one of royal rank. If a war breaks out and a fugitive kills him, then another fugitive enemy [will fall].

<column-break/>

...the same things. We shall see them from the walls. If he sees an enemy [in the form] of a snake <note>original: ὄφεως (opheōs)</note>, he will find good things and a portion of wealth from his enemy. <unclear>The roughness</unclear> of a python <note>original: πίθων (pithōn) — a large serpent associated with oracles and deep-seated wisdom or malice</note>: he will find a snake, both an enemy and wicked, but there is hope from the king in all these things. If he sees a corpse that seems to be forgotten, he will dissolve his fear of being oppressed by an enemy. And he will dissolve every burden of fear. Similarly, if he sees [a snake] dividing their kingdom, it points to the looting of his own error. If he sees a snake <unclear>doing wrong</unclear>, he will find an increase in his wealth and joy instead of bitterness. If he sees a corpse speaking to a snake, he will find joy, gladness, and peace from his enemies. If he sees a eunuch or female [serpents], he will find them among his enemies. He spoke of all those who are angry. If he sees a small snake [glowing] like fire, or carrying or having various colors around its knees, and it moves, he will find a king and master him. And this signifies a reign, or rather, he shall reign hereafter, being held by these mortal things. If he sees something like a deadly fire, or a bed resembling [a snake] that pleased such a person, he will find much gold or an ancient royal treasure <note>original: θησαυρὸν (thēsauron)</note. If he sees himself as if he went out into [the world] and wealth came out from others as small snakes, he will come to the mountains with an <unclear>ancient</unclear> [treasure]. And with fear, he will also strike his enemies. If he sees their dragon and they fled from it, he will be superior to his enemies. But if [the snake] <unclear>touched</unclear> him from wherever or his bed, he will find sickness and fear from an enemy. If it is a [droplet], judge it as a dialogue with an enemy.

## Preface to the interpretation of the Song of Songs

It does not seem at all [right] to me to ignore the grace [given] to you regarding matters of the divine oracles <note>original: λογίων (logiōn) — refers to the sacred scriptures as divine utterances</note>. These words are almost like ineffable secrets, and yet I dare to make some effort of zeal toward them. For I have been moved, in a way, by a passion for these most beautiful songs; their sacred clarity surpasses every spoken interpretation. These songs are the witness spoken of by the wise man <note>Referring to King Solomon, the traditional author of the Song of Songs</note>. How someone might contemplate the songs through the present work is what this speaks toward. 

But since it concerns the power of divine wisdom—the co-eternal Word <note>original: λόγος (Logos)</note> and the elder who shares the same throne—He who came for our salvation and took up our whole human nature, He raises the whole <unclear>gathering of reason</unclear> to the things above, according to the measure of the power given to him. It is as if one might say, having taken courage toward the world, as Paul says: **taking every thought captive to Christ**, imposing silence as much as possible upon [human] words.

<summary>This page contains a series of brief exegetical notes on the Song of Songs followed by a formal preface to a commentary on the text attributed to Clement of Alexandria. The preface emphasizes the ineffable and divine nature of the "Songs" and the role of the Logos in human salvation.</summary>

<keywords>Song of Songs, Clement of Alexandria, Logos, Paul the Apostle, Biblical Commentary, Divine Wisdom, Ineffable, Dream-visions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface attributed to Clement of Alexandria, which began on the previous page. The author is transitioning from a humble disclaimer about their own wisdom to a justification for interpreting the "Song of Songs" as an act of spiritual love (eros) rather than worldly ambition.</meta>

We have unfolded these matters in words to God. If, therefore, I have not shared in the good fortune of the wise, it is because He grants wisdom through grace to all alike, as is fitting for them. He commands that those who are being enlightened should not fail to sing out what they utter. Do not think that the wise man observes anything that is not fully contemplated, for nothing of His wisdom is withheld from anyone. We have set forth [these things] for the sake of grasping the divine nature; and may He be merciful to us, even if we have perhaps erred in those things where we might stumble—He who treats our failings with His **love for mankind**. <note>original: φιλανθρωπίᾳ (philanthrōpia) — a technical term in Greek theology for God’s inherent benevolence toward humanity.</note>

This has been fittingly gathered for us through everything belonging to the wise man and the prophet. For we have not dared these things for the sake of **ambition**, <note>original: φιλοτιμίας (philotimias) — literally "love of honor" or worldly recognition.</note> but for a heart with unclouded thoughts, for those who hold a **longing** <note>original: ἔρωτα (erōta) — a passionate, driving desire, here applied to the study of the scriptures.</note> for the **divine oracles**. <note>original: λογίων (logiōn) — refers specifically to the words of the Bible as sacred utterances.</note> It is like a drop of water falling upon a cold fire in the midst of a fierce fate; it stirs this up from—

<meta>catchword: that which [is] towards</meta>

---

—that which is toward the life of those [wise ones] within us. It is not cast down from the outside by those who happen to be the providers of what is happening. For this reason, a certain pain/grief <note>original: λυπηδὼν (lypēdōn)</note> has disturbed us, as if we were driven mad toward such a thing, especially not knowing <margin>not knowing</margin> the nature of the undertaking. 

And thus, let our whole life be compared [to this]: for **love is a tyrant**, <note>original: τύραννος ἔρωτος (tyrannos erōtos) — a common classical and patristic metaphor describing how spiritual or physical passion dominates the will.</note> pushing the one it has conquered quickly down a steep cliff. Nevertheless, to a friend, one does what is within one's power; and this passion within us is for the **learner** and the **philosopher**.

<summary>This page concludes the preface to a commentary on the Song of Songs, with the author justifying their work as an act of spiritual devotion and "divine eros" rather than personal ambition. The text ends by characterizing love as a powerful, "tyrannical" force that drives the seeker toward the divine.</summary>

Therefore, just as the breath of perfumes is the goodness of their scent, so the all-holy power of the Spirit is the "goodness" of all the intellectual powers. For the ointment was not poured out upon the Lord in the same way as it was upon the rest of the high priests—upon Christ, our high priest according to the order of **Melchizedek** <note>original: Μελχισεδὲκ — a mysterious priest-king from the Book of Genesis, seen by Christians as a precursor to Jesus's eternal priesthood.</note>, the great sacrifice—but rather the Holy Spirit, descending to come unto him, being the one who pours out every grace within him.

It "shades" every believer who was being scorched by the droughts of unbelief. It is likely called a "beautiful bed" because of the rest that comes to those who receive these mysteries, and the total stillness of a blessed life and a stable state for others.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on the Song of Solomon, specifically focusing on Chapter 4, verse 8. While the previous page discussed the "mountain of myrrh" (the soul's ascent), this page interprets the "Bride" as both the Church and, specifically in this Byzantine context, the Virgin Mary, as she escapes the "lions' dens" of worldly or demonic powers.</meta>

# Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon; you shall come and pass from the beginning of faith; from the head of Shenir and Hermon; from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. <note>Song of Solomon 4:8</note>

All power and glory belong to the all-holy and blessed Virgin and to the Lord. For this reason, the prophet <note>referring to Solomon, traditionally held as the author</note> has praised her with various names: sometimes as a "bed," at other times as a "house," and among other things. But here, calling her "bride," he says:

**"Come from Lebanon, my bride."** It is not obscure that she has attained rest and has been entirely deified <term>theized: made divine or filled with God</term> by the Sun. And as for the fact that through "Lebanon" he here indicates God, he places it as a symbol through the <unclear>comparison</unclear>. For he says, "the glory of Lebanon was given to him." It is as if he were saying: the court from Lebanon was set apart for him. 

**"You shall come and pass from the beginning of faith."** This means: you alone, being from the beginning of the faith, have spoken to life; and you shall pass through the threats of the enemy without being tested. "From the beginning of faith"—since you endured, and it is no small wonder that you passed through [these things] by the power of Christ God.

<column-break/>

**"From the head of Shenir and Hermon."** For "Shenir" <note>original: "Sanir," a mountain peak in the Hermon range</note> is among the mountains that were naturally formed as "beginnings." 

<margin>Another interpretation</margin> These were taken to be opposite the inhabited world. <margin>the</margin> They share the vastness of the sea and the like <margin>the</margin> parts belonging to demons. Hence, for us, the Virgin is the one who casts down the power of the adversary. She is not guarded [by worldly means] but by her own divinity, [escaping] from the mountains and other...

**"Come from the head of Shenir and Hermon; from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards."** This refers either to the kingdom and the "cutting off" <note>original: "katatomen," a pun on "peritome" or circumcision</note> of the race, and the **Jewish synagogues**, or to the evil demons. Or perhaps it refers to the flow of what is necessary; what remains of the [divine] presence [rescues us] from evil arts, as if one were being taught [to escape] from the lions—those opposing enemies. They are called "wild beasts" because of the dishonor of their judgment, from which they are driven toward [sinful] pleasure.

<margin>note</margin> **"Wild beasts."** But the divine father <note>likely referring to King David as the Psalmist</note> named them "beasts of beauty." Wherefore he says: "Do not deliver the soul that confesses you to the wild beasts." <note>Psalm 74:19</note> Thus there shall be peace again. For they used to call upon the divine [to save them] from the evil ones, and I love her; since the Virgin was the first to escape from their bonds.

...leading us into the good state, for the fragrance of the speech was like honey. **As the scent of your garments, as the scent of frankincense.** <note>Song of Solomon 4:11</note> We have been made fragrant by all the divine groves. <margin>18</margin>
**The Virgin** is addressed as a **locked garden**, a cultivated plot. On one hand, because she will blossom in the future with Christ, the Living One. This "son" <note>The author uses the masculine "son" here likely to refer to the fruit of her womb</note> brings this forth because of the harmony of her nature—**a sealed fountain**. ...wells of salvation." <note>Isaiah 12:3</note> And God caused him to remain. **Your shoots are a paradise, with the fruit of henna-flowers**, inasmuch as through Gabriel the divine news of the Gospel came to pass. She provided the perfect grace of those fruits for our delight. **Nard and saffron; cane and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon.** Having adorned herself through the apostles <note>The Greek *apostolai* (shoots/branches) is here interpreted as a reference to the *Apostoloi* (Apostles)</note>, the various beauties within her are enumerated. **Myrrh, aloes, with all the finest perfumes.** Through the **myrrh**, he signifies that the birth was mortal <note>referring to Christ's human nature and susceptibility to death</note>; but through the **aloes**, he showed that she also possessed the breath of immortality. ### Chosen from ten thousands
**Chosen.** <note>original: "ἐκλελεγμένος" (eklelegmenos). ### His head is the gold of Cephaz; his

<margin>Note well</margin>
**His head is the gold of Cephaz.** <note>original: "κεφάζ" (Kephaz). This is a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew "Paz," referring to a place known for the finest gold. For in many places, the use of **gold** is a riddle signifying that which pertains to **God**. **His locks are like fir-branches, black as a raven.** These clearly refer to the things above his head—that is, the things concerning his **divine existence**, which are unseeable and incomprehensible. ### His eyes are like doves,
### by the fullness of waters.

Just as his **Father** said previously: "Clearly, the **eyes of the Lord** are upon the righteous." <note>Psalm 34:15.</note>

### His cheeks are like bowls of spices,
### producing perfumes.

The writer offers "frankincense" to represent His divinity and His fragrance through the likeness of visible things. The things that come from His "throat" represent His gentleness and sweetness. <meta>This page continues the therapeutic discourse from the previous folio. Having established that memory serves as a "healing balm" for the despondent soul, the author now transitions to the method of gradual revelation. He argues that spiritual or intellectual light must be introduced slowly—bit by bit—so as not to overwhelm a person who has been weakened by "sickness" or previous hardships. This is presented as a "divine economy" or careful management of the soul’s recovery.</meta>

<meta>This page concludes the narrative of a visionary experience, identified by the vocabulary as the "Vision of Gregory" from the *Life of Basil the Younger*. It transitions from descriptions of a celestial paradise and the "Great King" (Christ) into a formal scribal colophon requesting prayers for the copyist.</meta>

Concerning the word of the King, as recorded in the new memoirs, a certain noble man handed down these sorts of things to them: he says that their beloved is beautiful and radiant in form. But as for the perch <note>original: πέρκι (perki); a type of fish, likely used here in a symbolic or allegorical sense within the vision</note> falling into the deep seas, one would not deny that upon returning, it suffered a seizure—much like those who care only for their bellies. He also speaks of the multitude of moray eels <margin>moray eel</margin>, which, when many are revealed, do not spare those of the day, nor are they mere phantoms. It seems they are restored toward the evening and do not sleep in the passage because of the moisture and the water, but rather they sail and spread out. He says also that the fish will not be without a share of human grace regarding the walls; and thus, having revealed the hymn, he says that he uncovered it. He tells also when he was seen and appeared, and in what manner, saying it was no less than the others.

He said these things as they were revealed, as one not fearing him. For this is how it was: the one who had invited him did not stand over him at the lighthouse <note>original: φάρει (pharei); can mean a lighthouse, a large cloak, or a specific location in Constantinople</note>, and he was revealed from his garment, either leaping and jumping or imitating the citizenship <note>original: πολιτισμόν (politismon); referring here to the way of life or conduct of the heavenly citizens</note> among them. And he said that many would desire secret things—for many do desire them—and many seek after his writings, his spirit, and his truth. I will not say "many" only, for they shall shine like a stone whose beauty cannot be surpassed, through a coloring of beauty and rays. For indeed, compared to the beauties and colors of this earth—such as emeralds, ointments, and salts—their beauties are unlike anything in the world. We might appear as if we cannot reach it; their eyes are not [merely] light, nor are their gates [simply] bright, nor are their walls [merely] gold. Yet they are with lights and spirit, arising from those things here. These things, then, I heard. Just as when I was on the mountain and remembered, I wept. He handed these things over last year. He spoke with his face above his eyes <note>perhaps referring to a radiant brow or a specific visionary gaze</note> and according to their tent at the lighthouse; and reclining, he smiled very sweetly. And as for his name, so that the nations might give it to him, they favored him with their right hand, or like those seeing ointments. They shall give amulets <note>original: φυλακτήρια (phylaktēria); protective charms or prayer-scrolls</note> upon their forearms. For their shouting did not save them. But he will stretch out his hand and fill the whole inhabited world, as it looks toward the Great King. And there is a remembrance of his freedom and his faith, when he is no longer merely human, he says, but God. And he will give to the one beside him the care over them and all his right hand, and his face exults, and his whole tension is toward the East, with a breath that no one knows. And then both the spiritual nature and the patience shall be known to him by the tempering of the spirit. For indeed,

<column-break/>

toward the continuations of freedom, he also left behind the old sorrows <margin><unclear>the old ones</unclear></margin> and left behind those who hate. And everyone who was there saw him, he says—all the poor and the needy. And then all the people in the world who had ceased, and the first men, were received by God. And with them were the angels, who are blessed and are as capable as bees <note>original: μελίσσιοι (melissioi); an image suggesting both sweetness and tireless, harmonious activity</note>. And they performed his whole will with their very lives. They would say: "Blessed are his people, and blessed are those who are with the Lord." For the sake of this one, God was well-pleased with the whole world and all the earth, so that the saints might know death. These blessed ones do not have their hope in this life alone, but also in the one to come. For the spiritual ones are tried by no small number of varied temptations and entanglements of life; yet against none of the many in this world did he raise his hand, even among those who exceeded [in malice]. But when the things to come arrive, they will not be like the things here; for these things shall not pass away. Nor does anyone know them according to [earthly] hope; for it is not possible to know the things that come through the same means. But as all things that happened to their bodies are borne by the spirit in the enjoyment of their deeds, then he himself holds all his life and his prize <note>original: βραβεῖον (brabeion); the award given to an athlete or victor</note> with God. And then the Lord will say to him that the whole world should answer him; for he holds toward eternity. And they said: "The end of the righteous was not in this life." But the one who has endured through toil and labor holds the crown and the glory with God. And after all these things, he turns to his Master, who saved all and preserved him, because He does not disdain salvation. "I shall wash away these things," he cries out. Therefore, we also, with much joy and faith in this deed, embrace the divine graces of the Spirit which contain the truth. For the Master did not withhold the Spirit from any of the saints, for even unto his imprisonment, he accepted death so that he might save us all. And all the earth shall be revealed to him, and his whole spirit shall be the Lord's. And they all said: "To him be the glory forever and ever, amen."

->IT IS FINISHED<-

As for the present book, and all its writing, glory be to the Holy God, and to his honor and glory. I hold for all time my hope in the Lord, throughout all the time of my life and my nature. After this, pray for me, the humble and sinful one, that I might receive from God the forgiveness of my failings through the intercessions of our most holy Lady the Mother of God <note>original: Θεοτόκος (Theotokos); the Virgin Mary</note> and of all the saints.

<meta>This page continues the visionary account of Gregory, a disciple of Saint Basil the Younger. It focuses on the "Vision of Theodora," where Gregory’s deceased fellow-servant appears to him to describe the soul’s journey through the "aerial toll-houses" after death.</meta>

<page-num>54v</page-num>

For not many days had passed since the time of her ascent into heaven. And behold, as I seemed to be sleeping, that blessed woman came to me. After greeting me, she began to recount to me the great and wonderful things that had happened. She said: "I have brought my belongings to these regions, and I have come to you also, to see you again." And as she spoke in this way, I was afraid once more. I walked about, intending to bring her again to a certain guard-post. And she said: "Indeed, I thought that having come from above once more..." but she did not listen further. For never had she spoken anything to me in such a manner. "And if you have come to this," I said to her, "then I tell you, do not be afraid anymore." + 
Yes, just as we used to walk together in the old days, so it was now; or so it seemed. Looking intently at her, I seemed to see that there was nothing strange or estranged about her; she was exactly as she had been at the end, possessing all her own features and her very physiognomy, just as she had when she still lived in the flesh. And I seemed to ask her, saying: "My Lady Theodora, as you ascended into heaven and passed the wicked and shameful guards and demons, who are called <term>toll-houses</term> <note>original: τελώνια (telonia); stations in the air where demons are said to interrogate the soul about specific sins as it ascends to God</note>, did you suffer nothing? 
For my master, Saint Basil, knew that the <term>toll-houses</term> in the air are terrible, wicked, and fearful." + And she said to me: "In truth, Lord Gregory, I saw and knew all these things, and how fearsome they are; and if one does not happen to have great help from God, and the protection and prayers of His saints, one cannot succeed in the ascent to heaven. The wicked and savage demons present the sins of each person in their nakedness; for they do not only possess and claim justice for malice, wickedness, and pride, but also for everything involving bodily sin. For they themselves are near us during our evil deeds, seeing everything; hence they record them with great care. I even reached their company outside the gates. Behold, as that blessed woman says: 'Neither light nor joy was with me, except that someone came and sent help; for I was grieving and mourning because of those wicked and savage demons.' And then she told me how she fled from them and came out again, and she spoke these things to me. And as I questioned her, she answered me in the way I am telling you: 'Do not grieve for me.' And again she said these and those things; it seemed she fled from them, and as I questioned her again, I heard these same things. And I spoke to her once more:"

<column-break/>
<page-num>55</page-num>

In this way, she spoke with me about the demon and how he partitioned the passage of our souls. From every side, the wicked and defiled things were raised against us, bringing grief to our souls and the fear of death and judgment; yet she defended herself toward heaven and vanished. Was there perhaps some kind of struggle? 
And he said: "For already at the gateway it was revealed where I, in my poverty, had traveled, saying, 'Oh, how she was with us <gloss>among us</gloss> every day!'" 
Truly, truly, you are mine and part of this [vision] of mine. + 
Therefore, the departure of the soul is the most important thing, concerning both the wicked spirits and the rulers of the darkness of this age. For if anyone is of this world, he knows those who have been justified; if he is of God, they have already meditated much on being enlightened by Him. + 
The holy Apostle advises us, saying: 
> Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. <note>original: 1 Peter 5:8</note>
Oh, how we are subject to this road, whatever fortune this road may hold. In this road, there are guard-posts + and there is a cause for why they were pleasing; for we also, like that blessed woman who has already departed her flesh, are sinners in sin, yet God helped me through her triumphs over her failings. For He who moves nothing shamelessly rescued her soul from the pain and the hands of the wicked spirits. No one should fear a terrible enemy opposing her, and they said: "If it were not for the protection of our Lady the <term>Theotokos</term> <note>original: Θεοτόκος; the Mother of God</note>..." + 
Flesh and blood are changed in each person; and there is no human who has not committed some small thing, whether a slip of the tongue, a disorderly stance, or an idle word. None of these will be placed in the earth with him; rather, many things convict us, and truly so. 
Hence, that which was said by the Prophet is true: "The man who fills up his deficiencies." And this man is the one who lives always in repentance and confession; there is nothing greater than this. For he has guarded against and saved himself from every sin, and freed himself from the rotten voice of sin. For the forgiveness of our sins has become a matter of transition and hope; and if the Spirit of the Lord enlightens a man, he is sprinkled with the blood of our Christ as it was of old and forever. For our good and noble works lead the way; and if any man has a good work, it will guide him into the heavenly members, having found total ignorance [of his sins] from us, and she is already carried along, and she herself is life.

<summary>Theodora describes her journey through the aerial toll-houses to Gregory, explaining that only the help of God, the Virgin Mary, and the prayers of the saints allow a soul to pass the demonic accusers. The text emphasizes that while all humans sin through "idle words," those who practice constant repentance and confession can be saved by Christ's blood.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the narrative of the "Vision of Theodora" found on the previous folio into a dense, mystical-philosophical treatise. --- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page marks a sharp transition from the Neoplatonic philosophy of the previous folio into a series of apocalyptic prophecies. This genre, common in late Byzantine manuscripts, often blends historical anxiety with messianic hope, using cryptic language to describe the fate of Constantinople (the "City of Seven Hills") and its eventual fall and liberation.</meta>

# The Prophecy of the Fallen City

And giving testimony <gloss><unclear>upon the</unclear></gloss> ... <unclear>their</unclear> <unclear>breaking them</unclear>; so as even to tear off the crests of the helmets; and having <margin>a</margin> surrendered much there; as on one hand even the things done by him; for having retreated for them again. And when that day was fulfilled; and it seems they came to the rescue of the tomb; and laying hands on them, and of those <unclear>who were hunted</unclear> ...

<margin>b</margin>
Challenging all the nations, they give to those of the ... then they were; the governor at that time held the city. They took possession there, having seized the name beforehand through his <unclear>tongue</unclear>. But if someone foretold the name of God; and those of the East, the high priest brought matters to him. But when it was necessary for him coming from the East; and since even him then in those days—since upon the dawn, having taken the **fair-skinned race** <note>original: τὸ ξανθὸν γένος (to xanthon genos); a famous Byzantine prophetic trope referring to a northern, "blonde" people destined to reclaim Constantinople from its enemies.</note>, who shall reach and arrive in the **City of Seven Hills** <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἑπταλόφῳ (en tē heptalophō); a traditional epithet for Constantinople, mirroring Rome</note>, and he shall possess it henceforth.

But the Italians and Latins all [go] toward the city; and not one of them is in it; and they all [go] toward it, divine, and it has nothing ... there henceforth. And having sat down for the remainder toward the east and the northern land, so as not to be left behind; because of their slanted and crooked and wicked deeds which they shall do in this city. And there are mounds of earth for those very people; and after a short while, their repentance. But if also in time—the **Bulgarians** shall come together with the **Turks**, and there shall then be a great lamentation; and indeed for those dwelling in the city.

But after a short while, it says, the following things shall happen: those not having repentance and the rulers shall stir up wars against all; because her <term>downfall</term> <note>original: ἔκπτωσις (ekptosis); a falling away or expulsion from a state of power</note> and her removal shall also happen; the builders of the <unclear>portions</unclear> of Byzantium; as quickly as possible of them; as someone has said of him. The end shall be, and their authority from the east even unto the west. Some of them no longer exist; and in his lawless religion; and indeed they shall be utterly put to shame alone. The same [city], ancient and much-lamented; their fear and their fall; which has also been testified to in the scriptures; from whence comes their end.

<summary>This page contains a series of apocalyptic oracles concerning the fate of Constantinople, predicting its capture by various nations (including the "fair-skinned race") and the eventual downfall of its rulers.</summary>
<keywords>Prophecy, Constantinople, Seven-Hilled City, Fair-skinned race, Bulgarians, Turks, Latins, Apocalypse, Byzantine history</keywords>
